documents.markdown:
# Task comparisons

Choose a comparison for the decision you need to make. Each page includes current
requirements, results, limits, sources, and evidence from the linked tool profiles.
The tables are documentation comparisons, not benchmarks.

- [Two Python linting workflows](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/ruff-and-pylint/): Both check Python code for mistakes and conventions. Pylint uses inference and optional plugins; Ruff provides built-in rule families. Check the rules and plugins your project needs before switching.
- [Linting and type checking work together](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/ruff-and-mypy/): Ruff checks lint rules, such as unused imports. mypy checks type consistency, such as passing text where a number is expected. Use both when you want both kinds of checks.
- [Linting and type checking work together](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/ruff-and-pyright/): Ruff checks lint rules. Pyright checks types and imports. They provide complementary checks.
- [Can you rebuild the program?](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/address-sanitizer-and-valgrind-memcheck/): AddressSanitizer requires a build with instrumentation. Memcheck instruments an existing executable on supported hosts. Both need you to run the program with useful tests, and their supported platforms and checks differ.
- [Java source database or compiled classes](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/codeql-and-spotbugs/): CodeQL runs queries against a database extracted from source. SpotBugs checks compiled Java class files for bug patterns. Their preparation and checks differ; a shared finding label does not mean equal coverage.
- [Security queries or a stated property](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/codeql-and-jbmc/): CodeQL looks for problems described by its queries. JBMC checks Java assertions and properties within configured bounds. Choose based on your question and modeling effort.
- [Check a trace or search for a failure](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/rtamt-and-psy-taliro/): RTAMT evaluates signals you already have against a requirement. PSY-TaLiRo searches system executions for a violation. A monitor can be part of that search, but does not generate test scenarios by itself.
- [Compare Python type-checking workflows](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/mypy-and-pyright/): Both check Python types using annotations and stubs. Align the target Python version, imports, and strictness, then investigate diagnostic differences on the same code. Neither replaces linting or runtime validation.
- [Compare package inventories and advisory matches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/trivy-and-osv-scanner/): Both match identified packages to vulnerability data. Compare extraction and advisory results for the same input; finding counts alone do not rank the tools. Trivy also offers separate infrastructure-configuration checks.

For another selection, [compare two or three tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/).

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/comparisons/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/comparisons.json).

documents.markdown:
# Can you rebuild the program?

AddressSanitizer requires a build with instrumentation. Memcheck instruments an existing executable on supported hosts. Both need you to run the program with useful tests, and their supported platforms and checks differ.

[Choose a memory-checking workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/address-sanitizer,tools/valgrind-memcheck).

## Requirements and results

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Field | [AddressSanitizer (Clang)](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/) | [Valgrind Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | Use AddressSanitizer when you can rebuild C or C++ code and want to catch memory errors while running tests or fuzzing. |  |
| What you need | C or C++ source, a supported Clang toolchain, and permission to rebuild and run tests. Compile and link with AddressSanitizer instrumentation; an existing executable alone is not enough. | An executable program and inputs that exercise it. Rebuilding is usually unnecessary; debug information improves reports. |
| What you get | A runtime report identifying a detected memory error, with stack and allocation information when available. |  |
| Checks and limits | It checks instrumented code that actually runs. A clean run says nothing about unexecuted paths, and not every kind of memory error is covered. |  |
| Where it runs | Supported Clang/runtime OS and CPU combinations. The documentation lists Linux, macOS, Windows, and other platforms with differences in available checks; verify the chosen target. | Supported OS/CPU pairs include Linux and FreeBSD. Darwin support has version limits; native Windows is not a maintained target. |
| Cost conditions | Free compiler/runtime component. No paid analysis edition is required; instrumented execution uses additional memory and compute. | Free Memcheck tool in Valgrind. No paid upgrade is needed for the memory checks described here. |
| Edition and scope | Clang/LLVM AddressSanitizer. Leak and stack-lifetime checks have platform and configuration limits. | Memcheck only; Valgrind includes other tools for different analysis tasks. |

## Comparison sources and evidence

### AddressSanitizer (Clang)

Docs checked 2026-09-22. Execution: recorded. The Windows example ran MSVC AddressSanitizer with compiler 19.44.35229 on native Windows Server 2022 x64 in CI. The faulty C fixture reported a four-byte heap-buffer-overflow write at bounds.c:5 and exited 1; the correction exited 0 with no output. This is evidence for the MSVC Windows route, not a Clang execution, fresh toolchain installation, ARM64 support, or unexecuted paths.

- [Current checks, usage, and platform limits](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [Project guide to C/C++ instrumentation](https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizer)
- [Runtime licensing](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/compiler-rt/LICENSE.TXT)

- [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/agent-knowledge/ci/42653327079/source.json)

# Security queries or a stated property

CodeQL looks for problems described by its queries. JBMC checks Java assertions and properties within configured bounds. Choose based on your question and modeling effort.

[Compare Java workflows and result types](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/codeql,tools/jbmc).

## Requirements and results

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Field | [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/) | [JBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jbmc/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | Use CodeQL to investigate security problems and data flow in a source project, or to write queries for a recurring coding problem. |  |
| What you need | Create a CodeQL database from source. Some language and extraction modes require a build; others support no-build extraction. Then run a selected query suite. | Supply compiled classes, an entry point, dependencies, and JBMC runtime-library models. Configure bounds and assumptions; running the Java application is not required. |
| What you get | Alerts identifying code locations and, for path queries, a possible route through the program. CLI analysis can save a SARIF report. |  |
| Checks and limits | Results depend on extraction, selected queries, and framework models. No alerts does not establish that the project is secure. |  |
| Where it runs | Windows, macOS, and supported glibc Linux hosts; architecture and language prerequisites vary. | A compatible JBMC release or source-build host, plus a JDK to compile examples. JBMC inherits CBMC build prerequisites; verify release-package availability for the host. |
| Cost conditions | Free for public repositories and eligible uses under the CodeQL terms. Standard private organization scanning requires a paid GitHub Code Security entitlement. | Free open-source verifier. No paid JBMC edition is required for this workflow. |
| Edition and scope | CodeQL CLI and query libraries; catalog license category describes the CLI. | JBMC within the CBMC project. The official introductory example uses an older version; confirm current options and class-file compatibility with the selected release. |

# Java source database or compiled classes

CodeQL runs queries against a database extracted from source. SpotBugs checks compiled Java class files for bug patterns. Their preparation and checks differ; a shared finding label does not mean equal coverage.

[Compare Java workflows and result types](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/codeql,tools/spotbugs).

## Requirements and results

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Field | [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/) | [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | Use CodeQL to investigate security problems and data flow in a source project, or to write queries for a recurring coding problem. | Check compiled Java classes for known bug patterns without running the application. |
| What you need | Create a CodeQL database from source. Some language and extraction modes require a build; others support no-build extraction. Then run a selected query suite. | Compile the project to class files or JARs and provide dependency classes when needed. Source and debug information improve navigation; install Find Security Bugs separately for its detectors. |
| What you get | Alerts identifying code locations and, for path queries, a possible route through the program. CLI analysis can save a SARIF report. | Bug-pattern reports identify a category, class or method, and available source location. Review the attributed code and supporting context. |
| Checks and limits | Results depend on extraction, selected queries, and framework models. No alerts does not establish that the project is secure. | Missing classes and unsupported patterns reduce the check. Find Security Bugs detectors require a separate plugin. |
| Where it runs | Windows, macOS, and supported glibc Linux hosts; architecture and language prerequisites vary. | Runs on a compatible JVM on Windows, Linux, or macOS. Check both the runtime requirement and analyzed class-file version against the selected SpotBugs release. |
| Cost conditions | Free for public repositories and eligible uses under the CodeQL terms. Standard private organization scanning requires a paid GitHub Code Security entitlement. | SpotBugs and the optional Find Security Bugs plugin are free open-source components. Security checks require adding the plugin, not purchasing an edition. |
| Edition and scope | CodeQL CLI and query libraries; catalog license category describes the CLI. | SpotBugs 4.10.4 documentation, with Find Security Bugs explicitly treated as an optional plugin. JVM bytecode support is not native-binary support. |

# Compare Python type-checking workflows

Both check Python types using annotations and stubs. Align the target Python version, imports, and strictness, then investigate diagnostic differences on the same code. Neither replaces linting or runtime validation.

[Plan a comparable type-checker trial](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/#compare-python-type-checkers).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/mypy,tools/pyright).

## Requirements and results

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Field | [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) | [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | Check whether Python annotations, calls, and return values agree in a configured project. |  |
| What you need | Provide Python files, type annotations, configuration, and relevant dependencies or stubs. No application execution or test harness is required. | Provide Python source, dependencies or stubs, and a pyrightconfig.json or pyproject.toml configuration. |
| What you get | Diagnostics name the file, line, type mismatch, and error code, such as arg-type for an incompatible argument. |  |
| Checks and limits | Any, missing stubs, untyped code, and suppressions can hide mistakes. A clean check does not validate runtime input or behavior. |  |
| Where it runs | A local or CI Python environment. The current getting-started guide requires Python 3.10 or later to run mypy. | Node.js command-line installation or the documented editor integration. |
| Cost conditions | Free open-source type checker. Local use does not require a hosted service or paid analyzer edition. | Free open-source checker. Pylance is a separate editor product with its own scope and terms. |
| Edition and scope | The mypy command-line type checker and its documented gradual-typing workflow. This entry does not cover general security scanning or runtime type enforcement. | The open-source Pyright checker; Pylance-specific editor features are excluded. |

## Comparison sources and evidence

### mypy

Docs checked 2026-09-26. Execution: recorded. mypy 1.18.2 on Windows with Python 3.13.15 checked the single-file greeting fixture under its supplied strict configuration. The faulty fixture produced arg-type and exited 1; the corrected fixture exited 0. Target code was not executed. This does not establish runtime correctness, missing-dependency behavior, or results for other configurations and Python versions.

documents.markdown:
# Check a trace or search for a failure

RTAMT evaluates signals you already have against a requirement. PSY-TaLiRo searches system executions for a violation. A monitor can be part of that search, but does not generate test scenarios by itself.

[Choose monitoring or falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/temporal-monitoring-and-falsification/).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/rtamt,tools/psy-taliro).

## Requirements and results

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Field | [RTAMT](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/rtamt/) | [PSY-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psy-taliro/) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | Use RTAMT to check recorded or streaming signals against a requirement about values over time. | Search a callable model for inputs that violate a requirement evaluated by your chosen monitor. |
| What you need | A compatible Python environment, named signals with timestamps, and a requirement written in Signal Temporal Logic (STL). Choose the timing semantics that match your data. | A callable model or simulator, monitoring backend, temporal formula, input ranges, and search budget. A MATLAB bridge is optional. |
| What you get | A robustness value for the requirement on the supplied trace. Its sign and margin help locate and interpret a violation. | Run objects retain evaluated inputs and costs. Model-based evaluations can also retain the trace, letting you replay the lowest-cost scenario and inspect its score. |
| Checks and limits | It evaluates observations you provide. It does not generate test scenarios, and a passing trace does not prove that every execution satisfies the requirement. | Cost meaning depends on the evaluator. A finite search with no violation is not a proof; preserve the seed, bounds, model, and monitor settings. |
| Where it runs | RTAMT 0.4.10 requires Python 3.8 through 3.12 and antlr4-python3-runtime 4.7. The example uses Python 3.12.16 and the pure-Python backend; the optional compiled backend adds CMake, compiler, and Boost.Python requirements. | A supported Python environment; monitor backends and external simulators can restrict operating systems. |
| Cost conditions | Free monitoring library, including the documented Python APIs. Simulator and trace-collection costs are separate. | Free Python toolbox. MATLAB is not required for a Python-only workflow. An external simulator, optional integration, or compute service can have its own costs and license requirements. |
| Edition and scope | Offline and online STL monitoring. Online future-time operators are bounded; timing, parser, and backend compatibility depend on the chosen release. | PSY-TaLiRo 3.1.0 documentation; supported temporal syntax depends on the chosen monitor. |

Docs checked 2026-09-21. Execution: recorded. Robustness at time zero was -5.0 for the violating trace and 1.0 for the correction; reproduction assertions passed and the process exited 0. documents.markdown:
# Linting and type checking work together

Ruff checks lint rules, such as unused imports. mypy checks type consistency, such as passing text where a number is expected. Use both when you want both kinds of checks.

[Run the shared Python recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/).

[Customize this comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools/ruff,tools/mypy).

Documentation comparison; shared labels do not establish equal checks or coverage.

| Use it for | Use Ruff to check Python files for unused imports, common mistakes, and coding conventions. | Check whether Python annotations, calls, and return values agree in a configured project. |
| What you need | Python files or supported notebooks and an installed Ruff command. Choose the target Python version and rules for your project. | Provide Python files, type annotations, configuration, and relevant dependencies or stubs. No application execution or test harness is required. |
| What you get | Diagnostics with a rule code and file location. Some rules offer fixes you can review. | Diagnostics name the file, line, type mismatch, and error code, such as arg-type for an incompatible argument. |
| Checks and limits | Checks depend on the rules you enable. Security rules need deliberate selection; use a separate type checker for type consistency. | Any, missing stubs, untyped code, and suppressions can hide mistakes. A clean check does not validate runtime input or behavior. |
| Where it runs | Windows, Linux, and macOS through supported binary distributions or Python packages. | A local or CI Python environment. The current getting-started guide requires Python 3.10 or later to run mypy. |
| Cost conditions | Free open-source linter and formatter, with no paid analyzer edition required. Editor integration and local checks do not require a hosted account. | Free open-source type checker. Local use does not require a hosted service or paid analyzer edition. |
| Edition and scope | Ruff's Python linter, including documented notebook support. Formatting is a separate operation. | The mypy command-line type checker and its documented gradual-typing workflow. This entry does not cover general security scanning or runtime type enforcement. |

documents.title: Understand static analysis methods
documents.description: Distinguish value approximations, symbolic paths, proof obligations, and data-flow reports.
documents.markdown:
# Understand static analysis methods

**Choose a method by the question and evidence you need.** The same program can produce a possible-error alarm, a modeled counterexample, a generated input, or a proof obligation. These results have different meanings.

## One bounds check, several questions

This C function is an illustration, not an executed analyzer example. Assume `values` points to `count` readable integers:

```c
int read_at(const int *values, unsigned count, int index) {
    if (index < 0) return 0;
    return values[index];
}
```

The lower-bound check leaves the upper bound unchecked. For example, `count = 4` and `index = 4` selects an element beyond the array. Add an upper-bound check:

```c
if (index < 0 || (unsigned)index >= count) return 0;
```

Pointer validity and the relationship between `count` and the actual allocation remain assumptions to establish at the call site.

## Abstract interpretation: which values are possible?

An analyzer approximates sets of program states using a tractable representation, such as value ranges. At the array access, knowing only that `index` is nonnegative does not establish that it is below `count`.

Prepare the entry point, machine model, input assumptions, and library models. Typical output includes inferred values and alarms where safety could not be established. An alarm can reflect a real error or lost precision; investigate it under the stated assumptions. Frama-C's Eva uses this approach for C runtime-error analysis. [Eva documentation](https://www.frama-c.com/fc-plugins/eva.html).

## Symbolic execution: which path conditions can be satisfied?

Symbolic inputs stand for many possible values. Following a branch adds a constraint. Here, a model can ask whether a path with `index >= 0` and `index >= count` is feasible, then supply concrete values satisfying it.

Prepare a harness, symbolic inputs, environment models, and exploration limits. KLEE works on LLVM bitcode and produces test inputs for explored paths. Replay a generated input against the intended program and harness to check what it demonstrates. Paths interrupted by resource limits remain unexamined work, not successful checks. [KLEE's function tutorial](https://klee-se.org/tutorials/testing-function/).

[angr](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/angr/) uses its own binary-loading and execution models. A symbolic counterexample is evidence about a model; a replayed failure is evidence about that concrete execution.

## Deductive verification: does the code meet its contract?

Write the required property and assumptions as a contract. For `read_at`, specify the readable array region and the permitted indices. A proof system turns the code and contract into logical obligations, including the array-access bound.

Prepare contracts, loop invariants where needed, memory/arithmetic models, and supported provers. A discharged obligation establishes the modeled claim under its assumptions. An unresolved obligation may need a stronger invariant, more solver effort, or a code repair; it is not by itself a counterexample. Frama-C WP generates and proves obligations for ACSL contracts. [WP documentation](https://www.frama-c.com/fc-plugins/wp.html).

## Data flow and taint: where can an input reach?

Data-flow analysis tracks how values move through assignments and calls. Taint analysis can also track influence through transformations that change the value. For this illustration, a rule could model an untrusted index as a source and array indexing as a sink, then examine the intervening checks.

Prepare the query's sources, sinks, propagation steps, barriers, and library/framework models. A reported path explains a modeled connection; it does not establish that every runtime path or framework behavior is represented. Local analysis stays within a function, while global analysis follows modeled connections across functions. [CodeQL's data-flow explanation](https://codeql.github.com/docs/writing-codeql-queries/about-data-flow-analysis/). See [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/) and [Psalm](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psalm/) for their specific setup and rules.

## Read the workflow label

Method names do not determine every catalog tag. Symbolic execution can explore a model of program behavior; a workflow can mix concrete execution and symbolic reasoning. Emulating a decoder is also different from running an entire application. Check each profile's inputs, execution model, and result rather than reclassifying a tool from one technique label.

Use [static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/) to choose an input route and [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) to compare claims. After a run, [review its findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) with the model and limits retained.

documents.markdown:
# Ways to do DAST

Describe a DAST test along several dimensions: a scan can be active, authenticated, and API-focused at the same time.

## Passive and active checks

**Passive checks** inspect existing requests and responses without altering them for the check. For example, a checker might identify a missing security header in an observed response.

**Active checks** send specially constructed requests and examine the result. They can investigate behaviors that passive observation cannot establish. Active testing can alter data or trigger expensive operations; choose an authorized test environment and scope accordingly.

ZAP provides both kinds of checks. Discovery is a separate step: a crawler finds places to test, while the scanner performs the checks. See [ZAP's scanning guide](https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/api/).

## Authenticated and unauthenticated tests

**Unauthenticated tests** exercise what a visitor can reach without logging in. **Authenticated tests** operate with a configured account or session to reach additional functionality.

A successful login does not guarantee the session stays valid throughout a scan. Different roles may expose different behavior. See [ZAP authentication methods](https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/getting-further/authentication/authentication-methods/).

## Browser and API entry points

For a website, discovery may follow links, submit forms, or use a browser to reach JavaScript-driven interfaces. For an API, a definition or recorded requests can provide entry points that have no clickable page.

These are ways to expose functionality to the test, not distinct security guarantees. See [Burp Scanner's crawl and audit model](https://portswigger.net/burp/documentation/scanner).

## API and protocol testing

[Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/) generates tests from OpenAPI or GraphQL definitions and checks responses. [RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) uses an OpenAPI specification to construct REST request sequences, including relationships such as creating a resource before reading it. Both require a running target and appropriate authentication; parsing a specification alone is not a dynamic test.

For a custom network or device protocol, [boofuzz](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/boofuzz/) lets you describe message fields and request order. It requires a suitable failure monitor and reset strategy. A generated input, an HTTP error, and a confirmed vulnerability are different results.

These workflows can find correctness and robustness problems as well as security-relevant failures. Compare the enabled checks and exercised operations rather than assuming every API tester supplies the same DAST rules.

## Related dynamic techniques

| Technique                                       | What changes                                                                   | Relationship to DAST                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Coverage-guided fuzzing                         | Generates inputs and uses execution feedback to guide further tests.           | Can test native or JVM functions and libraries, beyond web scanning. See [libFuzzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/libfuzzer/) and [Jazzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jazzer/). |
| Runtime memory checking                         | Observes memory operations during an execution.                                | Can detect memory defects; it is not an HTTP scanner. See [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) and [Dr. Memory](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dr-memory/).  |
| Runtime race detection                          | Observes conflicting accesses and synchronization between threads.             | Checks a different class of runtime defects from memory bounds or web requests. See [ThreadSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/thread-sanitizer/).                                         |
| Temporal monitoring                             | Evaluates supplied signals against a temporal specification.                   | A monitor does not generate a falsification search by itself. See [RTAMT](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/rtamt/).                                                                                |
| Model and temporal falsification                | Searches simulation inputs for a trace that violates a behavioral requirement. | Fits under dynamic analysis and can test controllers or hybrid systems without a security focus. See [the falsification guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/).          |
| Property-based testing                          | Generates inputs to test properties or assertions you define.                  | Can test functions or stateful behavior without targeting web security. See [Hypothesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hypothesis/).                                                            |
| Interactive application security testing (IAST) | Uses instrumentation inside the running application while tests exercise it.   | Adds an internal view rather than relying only on external responses.                                                                                                                                       |

For IAST terminology, see the [OWASP IAST verification guidance](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-devsecops-verification-standard/blob/main/document/TEST-003-Interactive-Application-Security-Testing-IAST.md).

[Verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) compares fuzzing, property-based testing, temporal falsification, and formal verification.

## Describe the test precisely

"An authenticated active scan of the HTTP API" explains more than "we ran DAST." Record the application version, roles, reachable endpoints, test configuration, and environment with the results.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/dast-approaches/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/concepts/dast-approaches.json).

documents.title: Model and temporal falsification
documents.description: Find simulation inputs that violate a requirement about how a system behaves over time.
documents.markdown:
# Model and temporal falsification

**Model falsification searches for a counterexample: an allowed input or initial condition that makes an executable model violate a requirement.** Temporal falsification uses requirements about behavior over time, often expressed in Signal Temporal Logic (STL) or Metric Temporal Logic (MTL).

These are dynamic analysis techniques because the search runs simulations and evaluates their traces. They commonly test controllers and cyber-physical systems. See the [ARCH-COMP falsification report](https://www.sosy-lab.org/research/pub/2019-ARCH.Category_Report_Falsification.pdf) for examples.

[Browse the model falsification tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/dynamic/?technique=Model%20falsification).

## A concrete example

Suppose a simulated motor must keep its speed below 3,000 rpm for a 20-second test. You allow the search to vary the load and command signals within stated bounds.

If one allowed input produces 3,050 rpm at second 12, that trace is a counterexample. The useful result includes the input that caused it, so you can replay and investigate the failure.

Temporal requirements can also describe a deadline or a sequence:

| Requirement pattern            | Example                                                              |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Always                         | Speed stays below the limit throughout the test.                     |
| Eventually within a time bound | The actuator reaches its target within two seconds.                  |
| Response                       | Every request during the test receives a response within one second. |

These are illustrative requirements, not executable formulas. A response near the end of a test needs enough additional observation time to assess its deadline.

## Monitoring versus falsification

A **monitor** evaluates a requirement on a trace you already have. A **falsification tool** searches for inputs that generate a violating trace, using a monitor inside the search.

The usual workflow is:

1. Expose a simulator's inputs and output signals.
2. Define the requirement, allowed inputs, and test horizon.
3. Simulate a candidate input and evaluate the resulting trace.
4. Use the result to choose further candidates until a violation is found or the budget ends.

Many searches minimize a **robustness score**, which describes how a trace relates to a requirement. Under the standard signed semantics used by Breach, a positive score means satisfaction, a negative score means violation, and zero needs care at the boundary. A score is not a probability of failure. See [Breach's monitoring and falsification documentation](https://github.com/decyphir/breach/blob/master/README.md).

## Tools in this wiki

| Tool                                                                | Environment                                                    | Cost notes                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Breach](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/breach/)         | MATLAB; Simulink or a simulator interface; STL                 | Free toolbox; MATLAB and model dependencies are separate.                                                          |
| [S-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/s-taliro/)     | MATLAB and Simulink; temporal-logic falsification              | Historical free GPL toolbox; exact license version and current distribution unverified. MATLAB costs are separate. |
| [PSY-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psy-taliro/) | Python harness; temporal monitoring through a selected backend | Free toolbox; external simulator costs depend on the integration.                                                  |

The language filter describes the harness or modeling ecosystem here. A Python harness can call a simulator implemented in another language if you provide a suitable interface. [PSY-TaLiRo's documentation](https://psy-taliro.readthedocs.io/latest/) illustrates the model, requirement, and search components.

## What a result establishes

**No counterexample found is not a proof that the requirement always holds.** It means this search did not find one within its bounds and budget. Results depend on the model, input representation, simulation accuracy, time horizon, and monitor semantics.

A counterexample also needs interpretation: replay it, check that the input is allowed, and confirm that the model and requirement reflect the intended system. A simulated failure is not automatically a demonstrated failure of the deployed system.

## How this relates to DAST and model checking

Web DAST usually tests a running application's security behavior through its interfaces. Model falsification tests explicit behavioral requirements and may have no security focus. Both fit under [dynamic analysis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-vs-dynamic/).

Model checking asks whether a model satisfies a property under stated assumptions and may return a counterexample. Simulation falsification searches for violations.

[Verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) compares these results with bounded model checking, deductive verification, fuzzing, and property-based testing.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/concepts/model-falsification.json).

documents.title: SAST vs. DAST
documents.description: Understand what static and dynamic application security testing can tell you.
documents.markdown:
# SAST vs. DAST

**SAST looks for security problems in code. DAST tests the exposed behavior of a running application.** They answer different questions and can be useful together.

SAST means **static application security testing**. DAST means **dynamic application security testing**. This wiki uses DAST primarily for web and API security testing, a common use of the term.

## A practical comparison

|                  | SAST                                                                                                                     | DAST                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Input            | Source or a supported compiled representation.                                                                           | A running application and reachable interfaces.                                                                                                      |
| View             | Code structure and modeled behavior.                                                                                     | Requests, responses, and observable behavior.                                                                                                        |
| Language support | Usually specific to languages and frameworks.                                                                            | Often independent of the server's implementation language.                                                                                           |
| Example question | Could untrusted data reach an unsafe operation?                                                                          | Does this reachable endpoint respond unsafely to a test input?                                                                                       |
| Example tools    | [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/), [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) | [ZAP](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/zap/), [Burp Suite Professional](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/burp-suite-professional/) |

## How to interpret findings

Treat a finding as evidence to investigate. Static analysis can flag a path that is not feasible in your application. Dynamic testing can miss a vulnerability when it never reaches the relevant endpoint or state.

An empty report means that the configured test did not report a problem. It does not prove that the application is secure.

## Choosing a useful combination

For a web application, consider code checks during development and runtime checks against a representative test deployment. Keep authentication, authorization, and business workflows in the test design; automated scanning does not replace them.

For a native library, static bug finding plus a fuzzer and a memory checker may be more useful than a web scanner. The target matters more than the acronym.

## Sources

- [OWASP source code analysis tools](https://owasp.org/www-community/Source_Code_Analysis_Tools)
- [OWASP DAST overview](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/06-verification/02-tools/01-dast/)
- [ZAP scanning and authentication guide](https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/api/)

Continue with [ways to do DAST](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/dast-approaches/).

For research on using SAST in practice, see [SAST adoption](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-adoption/) and [SAST in CI/CD](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-workflow/).

documents.markdown:
# Static analysis approaches

**Start with what you have: source code, a binary, a dependency inventory, or configuration files.** Tools can inspect each without exercising the target application's runtime behavior, but they answer different questions.

## Source code versus binaries

| Input type          | What the tool examines                                                                               | Examples in this wiki                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Source code         | Code structure, types, values, or possible paths, often with build and dependency context.           | [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/), [PHPStan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/phpstan/), [Clippy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clippy/)                              |
| Binaries            | Compiled artifacts. A tool might recover code for weakness analysis or identify embedded components. | [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/), [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/)                                                                        |
| Dependency metadata | Package manifests, lockfiles, or software bills of materials (SBOMs).                                | [cargo-audit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cargo-audit/), [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/), [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) |
| Container images    | Installed artifacts extracted from an image without running its application.                         | [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/)                                                                                                                                                    |
| Configuration files | Infrastructure definitions, Dockerfiles, or other supported configuration formats.                   | [Checkov](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/checkov/), [Trivy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/trivy/), [Hadolint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hadolint/)                                |

Use the catalog's **Input type** filter to browse [source analyzers](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Source%20code), [binary tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Binaries), [dependency tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Dependency%20metadata), or [configuration checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Configuration%20files). A tool with multiple input types has more than one documented workflow.

Input type and analysis mode are independent. [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) also takes a compiled program, but observes it executing and therefore belongs under dynamic analysis. A source analyzer can run build steps to prepare its input without dynamically testing the application.

For JVM class files, see [Java source and bytecode analysis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/). For native memory errors, compare [source, instrumented-build, and executable workflows](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/).

## What kind of answer do you need?

| Technique                           | Main question                                                                     | Example                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Linting                             | Does this code contain a suspicious construct or violate a selected coding rule?  | [ESLint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/eslint/), [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/), [Staticcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/staticcheck/), [PMD](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pmd/) |
| Type checking                       | Are values, calls, and operations consistent with the available type information? | [PHPStan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/phpstan/)                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Bug finding and security analysis   | Can the analyzer identify a defect or potential weakness from code behavior?      | [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/), [PVS-Studio](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pvs-studio/), [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/)                                                  |
| Binary weakness analysis            | Does the recovered code show a potentially vulnerable pattern?                    | [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/)                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Software composition analysis (SCA) | Do identified components match known vulnerability records?                       | [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/)                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Infrastructure policy checks        | Do selected resource definitions satisfy the configured policies?                 | [Checkov](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/checkov/), [Trivy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/trivy/)                                                                                                                           |
| Secret scanning                     | Do selected files contain candidate credentials or secret-like strings?           | [detect-secrets](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detect-secrets/)                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Formal verification                 | Can a stated property be established under the model and assumptions?             | [CBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/), [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/), [Dafny](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dafny/)                                                                  |

These categories overlap. For example, a linter can find real bugs, and an SCA tool can inspect binaries. The label describes the workflow, not a ranking of effectiveness.

[Understand static analysis methods](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/) explains value approximations, symbolic paths, proof obligations, and data flow through one bounds-check example.

## Configuration and secret checks

For Terraform or Kubernetes definitions, start with [configuration checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Configuration%20files) and read the supported format and policy list. For a Dockerfile, [Hadolint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hadolint/) examines Dockerfile instructions and embedded shell usage; an image vulnerability scan instead examines packages in the built image.

A policy report describes the supplied definitions under the selected checks. Passed, failed, and skipped checks are distinct; a passed scan does not establish that a deployed environment matches those definitions. [Checkov's quickstart](https://www.checkov.io/1.Welcome/Quick%20Start.html) shows this distinction in its resource-policy output.

[detect-secrets](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detect-secrets/) identifies candidate strings for review and tracks a baseline. A match is not automatically a valid credential, and a baseline is not remediation. Its current-file workflow also does not establish that Git history is clear. If an actual credential was exposed, follow the issuing service's revocation or rotation procedure; deleting a line does not invalidate it. See the [project's baseline and audit workflow](https://github.com/Yelp/detect-secrets).

These checks inspect different evidence from application-source semantics and package/advisory matching. Keep the input, selected method, and resulting claim separate when [reviewing findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/).

## Binary analysis questions

The same executable can support several kinds of investigation:

| Question                                              | Starting tool                                                                                                                                     | How to interpret the output                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What files or regions are embedded here?              | [Binwalk](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/binwalk/)                                                                                     | Candidate formats and offsets guide further inspection.                    |
| What code structure can be recovered?                 | [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/)                                                                                       | Disassembly and decompilation need analyst interpretation.                 |
| What strings can be recovered?                        | [FLOSS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/floss/)                                                                                         | Strings are leads; decoder emulation is distinct from a full sandbox run.  |
| Does this artifact match my patterns?                 | [YARA-X](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/yara-x/)                                                                                       | A match establishes the rule's condition, not malicious intent.            |
| What capabilities are suggested by the evidence?      | [capa](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/capa/)                                                                                           | Record whether the evidence came from the binary or an execution report.   |
| Does recovered code contain a known weakness pattern? | [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/)                                                                             | Review code recovery and the applicable checker assumptions.               |
| Do identified dependencies match advisories?          | [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/), [cargo-audit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cargo-audit/) | Component/version identification and advisory matching are separate steps. |

These tools complement one another. Start with the question you need to answer, and preserve locations and artifact versions when moving between them.

Use **What can it find?** to filter by the kind of problem, such as memory safety or known vulnerable dependencies. Read Checks and limits before comparing coverage: some categories depend on optional rules, annotations, or instrumentation. [Verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) explains what different results establish.

## CWE is different from CVE

A **CWE** describes a weakness class, such as an out-of-bounds write. A **CVE** identifies a specific publicly disclosed vulnerability. See the [CWE overview](https://cwe.mitre.org/about/index.html) and [CVE Program overview](https://www.cve.org/About/Overview).

cwe-checker looks for weakness patterns in recovered code; CVE Binary Tool identifies components and matches vulnerability records. A weakness warning does not need an existing CVE, and a component-to-CVE match does not prove exploitability in your application.

## Read language filters with the input type

For a source analyzer, a language tag describes code it can inspect. For a dependency scanner, the same tag can mean it reads that ecosystem's package metadata. A binary tool's coverage instead depends on architecture, format, and how well it can interpret the artifact.

Combine **Source code + Rust** to find Rust source analysis. Selecting **Rust** alone can also show tools that inspect Rust dependency inventories. Read the language note on each tool for the distinction.

Similarly, do not assume all features in a product share a language list. PMD's bundled CPD utility detects duplication across more languages than PMD's supplied defect rules cover.

## Research in context

[Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) uses the OCPP study to explain why report counts depend on project and analysis scope. [Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/) explores how the available artifact constrains quality measurements.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/concepts/static-approaches.json).

documents.description: Understand whether a tool reasons about code or observes software executing.
documents.markdown:
# Static vs. dynamic analysis

**Static analysis inspects a program without exercising its runtime behavior. Dynamic analysis examines actual or emulated executions, either live or through recorded traces.** These labels describe how analysis happens, not whether a tool only finds security issues.

## Two views of the same problem

Imagine a function that reads a file and copies its contents into a buffer.

- A static analyzer can inspect the possible paths and reason about a copy that might exceed the buffer.
- A dynamic checker can observe an invalid memory access when a test input actually triggers that copy.

The first gives evidence from a model of the code. The second gives evidence from an observed execution. Neither guarantees that every defect has been found.

| Question                                 | Static analysis                                                                           | Dynamic analysis                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| What does it need?                       | Source, bytecode, or another code representation, depending on the tool.                  | Executable software and a way to exercise or observe it, or recorded execution data.       |
| Does the target execute during analysis? | No. A build or extraction step may still be required.                                     | Live tools exercise the target; trace monitors can analyze data from an earlier execution. |
| What limits coverage?                    | Models, rules, language support, and analysis scope.                                      | Inputs, reached paths, environment, and instrumentation.                                   |
| Example in this wiki                     | [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/) | [Valgrind Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/)          |

## Where security testing fits

SAST and DAST focus on application security. Static and dynamic analysis also serve other goals, including finding correctness bugs and understanding runtime behavior.

[Static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/) explains source analysis, compiled-binary inspection, and dependency vulnerability matching. Use the catalog's Input type filter to distinguish them; the input's format alone does not determine whether the analysis is static or dynamic.

[SAST vs. DAST](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/sast-vs-dast/) explains the security-specific terms. [Ways to do DAST](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/dast-approaches/) separates web scanning choices from related dynamic techniques.

[Model and temporal falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/) covers simulation searches for violations of behavioral requirements, including requirements about timing. These tools belong under dynamic analysis because they execute models and inspect traces.

[RTAMT](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/rtamt/) and capa's [sandbox-report workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/capa/) can analyze recorded execution data without running the original program again. FLOSS's [decoder emulation](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/floss/) is also distinguished from a full-program sandbox run in this catalog.

## Sources

- [OWASP source code analysis overview](https://owasp.org/www-community/Source_Code_Analysis_Tools)
- [Clang Static Analyzer documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangStaticAnalyzer.html)
- [Valgrind Memcheck manual](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/mc-manual.html)

documents.title: Verification and generated tests
documents.description: Compare fuzzing, property-based testing, temporal falsification, bounded checking, and deductive verification.
documents.markdown:
# Verification and generated tests

**Choose the claim and evidence you need.** Testing can reveal failures on selected inputs. A successful formal proof can establish a stated property under the model's assumptions.

## Compare the approaches

| Approach                   | What guides the work?                                                      | What you get                                                                                          | Tools                                                                                                                                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Coverage-guided fuzzing    | Execution feedback helps choose and mutate inputs.                         | Inputs that trigger crashes, timeouts, or other configured failure signals.                           | [AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/), [libFuzzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/libfuzzer/) |
| Property-based testing     | You define input strategies and properties.                                | Failing examples, often simplified to make debugging easier.                                          | [Hypothesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hypothesis/)                                                                  |
| Temporal falsification     | A requirement evaluates signals over time, often producing a search score. | A simulation input and trace that violate the requirement, if found.                                  | [Breach](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/breach/), [PSY-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psy-taliro/)     |
| Bounded model checking     | A solver checks modeled executions within exploration bounds.              | Property results and possible counterexamples; completeness needs separate attention.                 | [CBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/)                                                                              |
| Static formal verification | Program models, specifications, annotations, and proof procedures.         | Proved properties, possible-error alarms, or unresolved proof obligations, depending on the analysis. | [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/), [Dafny](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dafny/)             |

These categories can overlap. A test harness is code that calls the target and checks its behavior. A fuzzing harness can check a property, and property-based testing can use execution feedback to choose inputs. Compare what inputs each method needs, how it recognizes failure, and what its result establishes.

## Measure and challenge the tests

[coverage.py](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/coverage-py/) records which Python statements and
branches ran. Reaching a line does not show whether an assertion checked its
result. [StrykerJS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/strykerjs/) makes selected changes to JavaScript
source and asks whether a working test suite rejects the changed program.
This source mutation differs from a fuzzer mutating input bytes.

The [test-evidence guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/) supplies small coverage and
mutation examples, including a test that reaches all code without checking
return values and a boundary assertion that detects a surviving mutation.

## One example, several checks

Imagine a message parser that should accept valid messages and reject invalid ones without corrupting memory.

- A fuzzer can mutate message bytes. A sanitizer helps turn a memory error into an observable failure.
- A property-based test can generate valid message objects and check that encoding followed by decoding recovers the original object.
- A verifier can check a stated buffer-safety or output property under the assumptions in its harness or contracts.

If the parser controls a simulated device, a temporal requirement might additionally say that every accepted command receives a response within two seconds. The falsification search varies simulated inputs to seek a violating trace.

These are illustrative checks, not claims that every listed tool accepts the same target or implements all four workflows.

## You need a way to recognize failure

Generated inputs are only part of a test. A **failure detector**, sometimes called an oracle, decides whether the result is wrong. It might be a crash, an assertion, a comparison with a reference implementation, or a temporal-logic monitor.

An incorrect result that returns normally can go unnoticed by a crash-only harness. This is why the wiki distinguishes a tool's finding categories from its **Checks and limits** note. See the [Hypothesis quickstart](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quickstart.html) and [AFL++ workflow](https://github.com/AFLplusplus/AFLplusplus) for concrete testing interfaces.

## Interpret the result precisely

**No failing test found** means the explored cases did not trigger the configured detector. It does not prove all possible executions are correct.

For bounded checking, inspect whether bounds exclude further behavior. CBMC's [unwinding guidance](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/faq/loop-unwinding.html) explains how unwinding assertions help assess that question.

For deductive verification, an unresolved obligation may mean an incorrect implementation, insufficient annotations, or solver limits. A proved property still depends on the specification and modeled environment. [Dafny's tutorial](https://dafny.org/latest/OnlineTutorial/guide) and [Frama-C WP](https://www.frama-c.com/fc-plugins/wp.html) explain that specification work.

Use the [comparison view](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fcbmc%2Ctools%2Fafl-plus-plus%2Ctools%2Fhypothesis) to inspect the setup and scope of three approaches side by side.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests.json).

documents.description: Static knowledge format, MCP tool inputs, evidence semantics, limits, and recommendation profiles.
documents.markdown:
# Agent knowledge reference

Start with [Use ToolWiki with agents](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/using-with-agents/) for setup.
All four tools return `snapshotRevision`. Document citations contain `id`,
`title`, `url`, `revision`, and `evidence`. These tools read data and do not
execute target programs, install analyzers, or write files.

## Static format version 1

The base path is `/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/`. `manifest.json` gives the format
version, snapshot revision, document count, and each exported file's path,
SHA-256, and UTF-8 byte count. The manifest itself is not in its file list.

`index.json` lists all published documents. `documents/{id}.json` contains each
structured record; `documents/{id}.md` contains its clean Markdown with absolute
links. `snapshots/{revision}.json` contains every record in one file. There are
no audit scratch files, drafts, or error pages in the export. Links to relevant execution
records are retained as citations.

Each record has `kind` (`tool`, `guide`, `concept`, `research`, or `page`), title,
description, canonical URL, revision, Markdown, sections, sources, and evidence.
Tool records also contain the validated `tool` metadata used by the website.
Section offsets are JavaScript UTF-16 string offsets into the record's Markdown;
the section includes child headings until the next heading of equal or lower
depth. Section IDs match website anchors.

Document revisions are SHA-256 hashes of their JSON payload without `revision`,
with object keys sorted recursively, two-space indentation, and one final newline.
Array order is preserved. Snapshot revisions use the same rule over the snapshot
payload. Manifest hashes instead cover the exact bytes of the exported files.
Hashes detect corruption and mixed files; they do not authenticate a publisher.

`evidence.documentationReviewedOn` is a documentation review date or `null`.
`evidence.execution` has a `status`, `scope`, and source URLs. A `recorded` status
is a reference to the named execution and environment, not a new execution by
the MCP server. `not-recorded` does not mean an example was run or failed.
Read the document for qualifications and illustrative examples.

## search\_knowledge

All inputs are optional. `query` defaults to an empty string and allows at most
300 characters. Every query term must occur in the title, ID, description,
aliases, search terms, or body; title matches rank first. There is no embedding
service or semantic search. Results are sorted deterministically.

`filters` accepts `kind`, `language`, `input`, `mode`, and `finding`. Values are
case-sensitive and enumerated by the tool schema. Except for `kind`, these are
tool metadata filters and exclude guides. Unknown fields or values are errors.
`offset` defaults to 0 and is at most 2000. `limit` defaults to 8, from 1 to 20.
Results include the match count and `nextOffset` (`null` when complete).

```json
{ "query": "Python", "filters": { "kind": "guide" }, "limit": 5 }
```

## get\_document

`id` is required. Obtain it from search or the snapshot resource. Optional
`section` selects a returned section ID. `offset` defaults to 0; `maxChars`
defaults to 20000 and must be between 1000 and 40000. Offsets are within the
selected section when one is given. The maximum offset is 200000.

The response includes Markdown, sources, all section IDs, total character count,
and `nextOffset`. Pagination can split a code block; join all chunks before
executing commands. Unknown IDs, sections, or offsets beyond the selected
content return errors.

```json
{ "id": "guides/python-checks", "section": "prepare-an-isolated-environment" }
```

## compare\_tools

`ids` is required and accepts two to four distinct tool document IDs. Every ID
must identify a tool profile. The result uses the website comparison fields,
including setup, environment, result, scope, cost, sources, and limitations.

```json
{ "ids": ["tools/ruff", "tools/mypy"] }
```

## recommend\_checks

`profile` is required and uses the version-1 JSON exported by
[Find tools for your system](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/analysis-suite/). The server validates it
with the same schema and evaluates it with the same rules as the website.
Unknowns remain unknown; omitted prerequisites do not imply permission or
support. Profile goals are retained for compatibility and do not filter matches.

Here is a complete small profile for Python source on Windows. Empty strings,
empty lists, `inputsComplete: false`, and `unknown` intentionally leave details
unconfirmed:

```json
{
  "profile": {
    "version": 1,
    "name": "Python example",
    "preferences": { "cost": "", "license": "" },
    "components": [{
      "id": "app", "name": "Application", "included": true,
      "kind": "Command-line application", "languages": ["Python"],
      "inputs": ["Source code"], "inputsComplete": false,
      "goals": [], "notes": "", "binaryFormat": "",
      "hostPlatform": "Windows", "targetPlatform": "Windows",
      "deployment": "Local/desktop", "technologies": [],
      "access": {
        "rebuild": "unknown", "instrument": "unknown",
        "harness": "unknown", "testInstance": "unknown"
      }
    }],
    "connections": []
  },
  "limit": 10
}
```

Optional `subjectId` selects an included component or connection. `offset`
defaults to 0 and is at most 20000; `limit` defaults to 10 and ranges from 1 to
20\. Results include paginated matches, subject descriptions, gaps, and citations.
Each match includes its `candidate`, `details`, or `blocked` status and the
associated reasons or unanswered questions. Gaps include at most 20 summary
reasons with a `totalReasons` count; paginate matches for the complete per-tool
details. Profiles allow at most 50 components and 100 connections.

## Resource and error behavior

`toolwiki://snapshot` is a read-only MCP resource containing the current snapshot
revision and document inventory. Use `get_document` to read its records.

Tool responses are limited to 120000 UTF-8 bytes. Narrow the request or lower
`limit` or `maxChars` if the result exceeds that bound. Snapshot files are limited
to 16 MiB and remote reads have a 15-second timeout. Remote exports require
HTTPS; HTTP is accepted only on localhost for testing. Redirects are rejected.

Invalid arguments are rejected by the MCP schema; domain errors return an error
result. Startup rejects malformed manifests, unsupported versions, invalid
records, duplicate IDs, mismatched revisions, and altered snapshot bytes.
The server holds a validated immutable snapshot until restarted.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/agents-reference/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/agents-reference.json).
