documents.markdown:
# Check API descriptions and consumer contracts

An API description, a consumer expectation, and a running provider can disagree.
This guide checks two of those boundaries with an isolated parcel API example.

| Question                                              | Check                                                           | Deliberate fault                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Does the document follow a selected convention?       | [Spectral](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spectral/) | The GET operation has no `operationId`.                                     |
| Does the provider satisfy the consumer's interaction? | [Pact JS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pact/)      | The provider returns numeric `status: 7` where the consumer needs a string. |

## Prepare the example

Use the repository's
[`examples/api-contracts`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/api-contracts)
directory. It pins Spectral CLI 6.17.1 and Pact JS 17.1.4 with a package lock.
Use Node.js 22 or newer on a platform supported by Pact Core's native packages.
The retained run used **Node.js 24.22.1 x64 on Windows ARM64 through emulation**;
the locked Pact Core package does not supply a Windows ARM64 native binary.

From the example directory, install only its dependencies:

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
npm test
```

The fixture uses prebuilt native packages, so it needs no installation scripts.
Its runner disables Pact install tracking for subprocesses. It creates a Pact
mock provider and a small test provider on loopback with available ports, then
closes them. It does not require a broker, credentials, or an external endpoint.

## Read the document-lint result

The `.spectral.yaml` ruleset contains one rule, `operation-id-required`, that
checks GET operations. `openapi.bad.json` omits the field;
`openapi.good.json` adds `operationId: "getParcel"`.

The retained run produced:

| Case               | Exit code | Observation                                                       |
| ------------------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Faulty document    | 1         | One `operation-id-required` diagnostic at `paths./parcels/1.get`. |
| Corrected document | 0         | An empty diagnostic array.                                        |

The runner writes `reports/spectral-bad.json` and `reports/spectral-good.json`
using Spectral's output-file option. Console output can contain an additional
informational message, so do not parse the entire console stream as JSON.

This ruleset is deliberately small. A passing result does not establish full
OpenAPI validity, successful client generation, or agreement with a real server.
When adapting the example, preserve the project's existing ruleset and failure
threshold unless a specific change is intended.

## Read the contract result

`consumer.mjs` describes a GET request for parcel 1 and calls `parcelStatus()`
from `client.mjs` against Pact's mock provider. The returned object must have an
integer ID and a string status, and the consumer asserts its uppercase result.
A successful consumer run generates `reports/pacts/ParcelClient-ParcelAPI.json`.

`provider-check.mjs` reads that generated file and verifies a local provider.
The faulty variant returns a number for `status`; the correction returns the
string `queued`. The static fixture already supplies parcel 1, so its provider
state handler performs no setup. Replace that handler with appropriate state
preparation when adapting the test to a real provider.

The retained run produced:

| Case               | Exit code | Observation                                                                   |
| ------------------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Consumer test      | 0         | The actual client agreed with the mock interaction and generated a pact file. |
| Faulty provider    | 1         | A body-type mismatch at `$.status`: integer `7` did not match a string.       |
| Corrected provider | 0         | The provider satisfied the one supplied interaction.                          |

The verifier checks that exact mismatch, not just any nonzero exit. A missing
native binary, provider startup error, or malformed contract must not be counted
as evidence that the intended defect was detected.

## Keep the evidence and choose the next check

The overall `npm test` exits zero only when all five expected outcomes occur.
It writes commands, tool/runtime versions, source hashes, output, and scope to
`reports/`. The [retained run](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/audits/api-supply-tools/evidence/api-contracts)
records the executed fixture, not a benchmark or cross-platform certification.

A consumer pass alone says nothing about the real provider. A provider pass
only covers the supplied interactions and matching rules. Keep consumer,
contract, and provider versions together when investigating a regression.

Use [Schemathesis and the disposable API guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/) to generate
additional requests from an API definition. Use [finding review](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/)
to distinguish an expected policy failure from a broken check. An API document
and a generated Pact contract have different roles; one does not replace the other.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-contracts/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/api-contracts.json).

- **Documentation reviewed:** Not recorded
- **Execution evidence:** recorded
- **Execution scope:** November 12, 2026 run of Spectral CLI 6.17.1 and Pact JS 17.1.4 with Pact Core 20.2.0 on Windows using Node.js 24.22.1 x64. One custom lint rule and one local HTTP interaction were checked, including faulty and corrected variants. No external target, broker, or result publication was used.
- [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/api-supply-tools/evidence/api-contracts/run.json)

documents.title: Test a disposable HTTP API
documents.description: Reproduce a known API failure, correct it, and inspect generated tests against the same schema.
documents.markdown:
# Test a disposable HTTP API

Use this small orders service to try [Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/)
and [RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) against a known fault. The service, schema,
and replay script are maintained in [examples/http-api](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/http-api).
[Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/) first. Run the commands from the extracted
repository root unless a step names another working directory.

The service binds to `127.0.0.1:8771`. It has no credentials or external services.
Requests create and delete in-memory orders; reset or restart clears them.
The HTTP fixture is separate from boofuzz's custom-protocol harness.

## Start and reproduce the fault

Use **Python 3.13** for this walkthrough. Check the interpreter in PowerShell
before creating an environment:

```powershell
$apiPython = (Get-Command python).Source
& $apiPython --version
```

Expect `Python 3.13.x`; the new execution record uses **3.13.15**. If the command
is missing or reports another version, install/select Python 3.13 and set its
full executable path, then repeat the check:

```powershell
$apiPython = 'C:/PATH/TO/Python313/python.exe'
& $apiPython --version
```

Replace `C:/PATH/TO/Python313/python.exe` with your installed interpreter. Optional:
see [Python on Windows](https://docs.python.org/3.13/using/windows.html) for setup.
Schemathesis 4.33.1 declares [Python 3.11 or newer](https://github.com/schemathesis/schemathesis/blob/v4.33.1/pyproject.toml)
as its minimum; that is separate from the versions tested here.

The service uses only the Python standard library. Create the environment once
and start the faulty service in this terminal:

```powershell
& $apiPython -m venv .preview/api-demo-env
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/server.py
```

Wait for `Ready on http://127.0.0.1:8771`. In a second terminal, run:

```powershell
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/replay.py
```

This sends `POST /orders` with `{"quantity": 0}`. Zero is valid in the schema,
but the faulty implementation divides the order total by its quantity. The
observed response is HTTP 500. The replay command exits successfully when it
reproduces this expected fault; its exit status is not an API health verdict.

A positive quantity creates an order and returns an `id`. That value is consumed
by `GET /orders/{orderId}` and `DELETE /orders/{orderId}`. The schema declares
these producer/consumer links. Deleting an order makes later reads return 404.

Reset between independent runs:

```powershell
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/replay.py --reset
```

Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Restart in corrected mode and check the same input:

```powershell
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/server.py --fixed
```

```powershell
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/replay.py --expect-fixed
```

The corrected implementation uses the known unit price. The observed response
is HTTP 201 with total zero and unit price ten; the script then reads back the
created order. Use Ctrl+C to stop it when finished. A refused connection means
the service is not ready or the port is wrong, not that a test passed.

## Run Schemathesis

The demo selects the coverage phase, positive generation, and
`not_a_server_error`. It asks whether generated schema-valid inputs trigger a
server error. This does not cover every request, business rule, or security
property.

Install the pinned dependencies into the environment you created. Start the
faulty service, then run the check in the second terminal:

```powershell
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python -m pip install -r examples/http-api/requirements-lock.txt
.preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/python examples/http-api/run_schemathesis.py --output .preview/api-faulty
```

Then stop the service, start `--fixed`, and repeat the wrapper command with
`.preview/api-fixed` as the output directory. Use a fresh directory for each
run. The wrapper retains stdout, stderr,
JUnit, the exact CLI command, and process status. It sets UTF-8 only for the
child process so captured output also works on Windows. Stop the service with
Ctrl+C when finished. Linux/macOS execution was not tested; the environment's
executables live under `bin` instead of `Scripts` on those hosts.

**Historical execution, 2026-11-06:** Schemathesis 4.33.1 on Windows/Python
3.12.16 exited 1 against the faulty service and 0 against the corrected service.
The [original execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/remaining-work/executions/http-api/record.json)
retains those results and input digests.

**New execution, 2026-11-06:** A fresh Windows/Python 3.13.15 environment installed
the same lockfile and reproduced both results. The faulty run stopped at its
first server-error finding, leaving two operations untested. The corrected run
tested all three operations in the selected phase without a finding. See the
[new execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/7fce8e2cf1903a98cade96865bb383036f200e13/audits/reader-workflows/implementation/api/record.json).
A later short run need not discover the fault; `replay.py` is the deterministic
check.

See the [CLI reference](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/cli/)
for check selection, limits, reports, and exit-code meanings. Failure to load a
schema or complete setup is different from a failing API response.

## Adapt to your API

Use the pinned CLI directly with your API's OpenAPI file and a disposable local
service. In this example, `./widgets.json` is your saved schema in the repository
root, `http://127.0.0.1:8781` is the running test API's base URL, and the exact
path/method filters select only `POST /widgets`. Replace those three values to
match your service; include any API base path in `--url`. Filters select schema
operations; capability probes and negative method cases can send other requests.

From the repository root in **PowerShell 7**, run a bounded positive check:

```powershell
$out = '.preview/api-custom-positive'
if (Test-Path $out) { throw 'Choose a new report directory.' }
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $out | Out-Null
$priorEncoding = $env:PYTHONIOENCODING
try {
    $env:PYTHONIOENCODING = 'utf-8'
    & .preview/api-demo-env/Scripts/schemathesis.exe --no-color run ./widgets.json `
        --url http://127.0.0.1:8781 --include-path /widgets --include-method POST `
        --phases coverage --mode positive --checks not_a_server_error `
        --max-time 20 --workers 1 --max-failures 1 --request-timeout 3 `
        --seed 20261106 --report junit --report-junit-path "$out/junit.xml" `
        1> "$out/stdout.txt" 2> "$out/stderr.txt"
    $LASTEXITCODE | Set-Content "$out/exit-code.txt"
} finally {
    $env:PYTHONIOENCODING = $priorEncoding
}
```

This gives the run a 20-second budget, one worker, a stop after one failure/error,
and a three-second request timeout; the budget is not a hard process deadline.
Inspect `stdout.txt`, `stderr.txt`,
`exit-code.txt`, and `junit.xml` for findings and skipped work. The shell restores
its previous output encoding setting afterward. Keep this command with your
[run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/); choose a fresh `$out` for every run.

To ask whether the API rejects **schema-invalid input**, repeat the block with
`$out = '.preview/api-custom-negative'` and replace its generation/check line:

```powershell
        --phases coverage --mode negative --checks negative_data_rejection `
```

The positive server-error check does not test invalid-input rejection.
`negative_data_rejection` evaluates rejection of invalid generated inputs; it
accepts certain error statuses, including 5xx, so use `not_a_server_error` too
when checking that rejection avoids server errors. For both kinds of input in one run,
use `--mode all --checks not_a_server_error,negative_data_rejection`. See the
[check definitions](https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/checks/).

The new execution record tests the two separate commands against a scratch
variant of the supplied fixture: `/orders` became `/widgets`, with a saved
`widgets.json` and port 8781. Positive testing found the faulty zero-quantity
500 and passed after correction; negative testing exercised invalid requests.
The record lists the actual requests, results, and limitations. The combined
`all` variant, authentication, and real services were not tested.

## Use the same service with RESTler

**Illustrative; RESTler was not executed.** This route follows
[RESTler 9.3.1](https://github.com/microsoft/restler-fuzzer/tree/v9.3.1), whose
local build instructions name Python 3.12.8 and .NET 8 on 64-bit Windows or Linux.
Build that tagged checkout with its documented prerequisites before continuing.

Start the orders service in faulty mode. In a separate empty working directory,
run the tagged quickstart with absolute paths to its script, this schema, and
your RESTler build directory. In PowerShell:

```powershell
python C:/src/restler-fuzzer/restler-quick-start.py --api_spec_path C:/src/ToolWiki/examples/http-api/openapi.json --restler_drop_dir C:/src/restler_bin --ip 127.0.0.1 --port 8771 --task test
```

Replace the three `C:/src` paths with your checkout and build locations. Test
mode compiles the schema and sends requests. It does not just inspect the file.
The schema's [OpenAPI links](https://github.com/microsoft/restler-fuzzer/blob/v9.3.1/docs/user-guide/Annotations.md)
connect the returned order ID to read and delete requests.

Inspect `restler_working_dir/Test/RestlerResults/experiment*/logs/testing_summary.json`
and the network log. Confirm that resource creation succeeds and that read and
delete requests use the returned ID. Compilation alone, failed resource
creation, or setup errors do not establish successful API testing. Preserve
the generated `Compile` directory and logs.

After that smoke test works, reset the service and use a separate result
directory for a bounded fuzz run. For example, from `restler_working_dir`:

```powershell
dotnet C:/src/restler_bin/restler/Restler.dll fuzz --grammar_file Compile/grammar.py --dictionary_file Compile/dict.json --settings Compile/engine_settings.json --target_ip 127.0.0.1 --target_port 8771 --no_ssl --time_budget 0.01
```

The requested budget is 0.01 hours. A request or cleanup can finish after the
budget expires. Keep the server running until RESTler exits; Ctrl+C stops the
server afterward. This small run is for learning, not an exhaustive search.

Review [bug buckets and replay logs](https://github.com/microsoft/restler-fuzzer/blob/v9.3.1/docs/user-guide/Fuzzing.md),
then replay any candidate failure. Repeat against `--fixed` in a fresh result
directory. A short run without findings does not prove that defects are absent. Raw
finding counts do not compare RESTler and Schemathesis coverage.

Use a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/) to retain target mode, schema and code digests,
tool/dependency versions, limits, commands, setup failures, reports, and replay
results. The [finding review guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) explains how to decide
whether a failure belongs to the implementation, schema, or test setup.

For response-time and error thresholds under a defined local workload, use the
[k6 example](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/k6/#first-try) with the corrected service. It asks a
different question from generated API input testing.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/api-testing.json).

documents.title: Check browser behavior and accessibility
documents.description: Reproduce a search regression and missing-label issue, then verify the corrected local page with Playwright and axe-core.
documents.markdown:
# Check browser behavior and accessibility

[Playwright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/playwright/) checks browser behavior against assertions
you write. [axe-core](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/axe-core/) evaluates automated accessibility
rules in a rendered page state. This example gives each tool a separate fault
to detect in a small search page.

The [example files](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/browser-testing)
are separate from the live ToolWiki application. The fixture binds only to
`127.0.0.1:8837`, uses no credentials, and has no external services. Its links
point to ToolWiki profiles, but the tests check their destinations without
navigating to them.

## Prepare the isolated example

[Get the repository examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/), then use Node.js 24 and
pnpm 11.25.0. From the repository root:

```sh
cd examples/browser-testing
pnpm install --ignore-workspace --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run install:browser
```

The install command uses this example's lockfile. The browser script downloads
the Chromium build expected by Playwright into this example's `.browsers/`
directory. It does not replace the browser you use for normal browsing. On
Linux, [Playwright's browser dependencies](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#install-system-dependencies)
may also need to be installed for your distribution.

The recorded execution used Node.js 24.22.1, Playwright Test 1.65.0,
`@axe-core/playwright` and axe-core 4.14.0, and Chromium 158.0.8127.18 on a Windows
ARM64 host. The downloaded browser was the win64 distribution. Other supported
hosts are documented upstream but were not run for this example.

## Reproduce both faults

Run the unchanged tests against the faulty page:

```sh
pnpm test:bad
```

Expect exit status 1 and two failing tests:

| Check                 | Observed failure                                                     | Meaning                                                          |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Capability search     | The `memory` query left zero visible results where one was expected. | The faulty filter examines tool names but omits capability text. |
| Initial-page axe scan | Rule `label` identified `#tool-query`.                               | The input lacked an accessible name in this rendered page.       |

The runner starts and stops its own local server. If port 8837 is already in
use, it refuses to reuse that service. A missing browser, server failure, timeout,
or other infrastructure error is not evidence that either intended fault was
detected.

Full test output and axe attachments are written to `.results/bad/report.json`.
The failure screenshots and error context are under `.results/bad/artifacts/`.
These files are regenerated by later runs of the same variant.

## Apply the corrections and repeat

The corrected page makes two small changes: it searches the visible tool and
capability text, and it adds an explicit label associated with the search input.
Run the same test file against that version:

```sh
pnpm test:good
```

Expect exit status 0 and two passing tests. In the recorded run, `memory`
retained the AddressSanitizer result and its profile URL, and a case-insensitive
name query retained mypy. The initial-page axe scan had no violations or
incomplete results for the selected rule tags.

To verify the complete before-and-after exercise and create a compact record:

```sh
pnpm verify
```

The verifier requires exactly the two intended failures on the faulty page and
two passes on the corrected page. It checks that a browser actually started,
that the capability failure was the result-count assertion, and that axe
reported `label` for the faulty page. It writes `.results/verification.json`
with versions, commands, process statuses, input hashes, and rule-result IDs.
The [retained execution](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/browser-testing/record.json)
and [audit notes](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/browser-testing/README.md)
describe the run used by this guide.

## Understand the tested scope

The behavior test checks a small search contract at one viewport. It does not
exercise every query, browser, device, navigation route, or interaction. The
accessibility test scans the initial page with `wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`,
and `wcag21aa` tags. It does not scan the filtered states from the behavior test.

A scan without violations is not a full accessibility assessment. Inspect any
`incomplete` results, exercise additional states, and include manual keyboard,
screen-reader, zoom, and user assessment for the real application.
[Playwright's accessibility guide](https://playwright.dev/docs/accessibility-testing)
explains these limits and the axe integration.

## Adapt this to an existing application

Keep the project's browser configuration, locked tool versions, test projects,
and test-data reset procedure. Use a browser-renderable test UI, then write
assertions for the visible outcomes users need. The system builder's
**Browser UI** technology describes this requirement; a running backend or
command-line process alone does not satisfy it.

Prefer [role and label locators](https://playwright.dev/docs/locators) where they
represent the application's user-facing contract. This example uses a test ID
to reach the deliberately unlabeled input so the behavior and accessibility
failures remain independent. That test ID does not supply an accessible name.

Retain the application revision, browser build, viewport, selected states,
assertions, axe version, and rule tags in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Keep
assertion failures and incomplete execution distinct when deciding how to
[handle checks in CI](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/).

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/browser-testing/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/browser-testing.json).

- **Documentation reviewed:** Not recorded
- **Execution evidence:** recorded
- **Execution scope:** Windows ARM64 host (kernel build 10.0.26300) with Node.js 24.22.1, Playwright Test 1.65.0, axe-core and @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0, and bundled win64 headless Chromium 158.0.8127.18. One 1000x720 viewport, authored search assertions, and the initial page's selected WCAG rule tags. Both faulty checks failed for their intended reasons and both corrected checks passed. No other browser/platform or manual accessibility assessment was executed.
- [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/browser-testing/record.json)

documents.title: Record a tool choice
documents.description: Preserve why a shortlisted tool fits a component, what it needs, and which questions still need answers.
documents.markdown:
# Record a tool choice

Use this note to turn a shortlisted tool into an evaluation plan for one
component or connection. It does not change the system
builder's exported description or the three-tool comparison limit.

## Make the choice explicit

Copy this template into your project:

```text
Component or connection:
Question to answer:
Chosen tool, edition, and workflow:
Input and intended environment:
Why this workflow fits:
Alternatives or complementary tools considered:
Required access, setup, and dependencies:
Unresolved compatibility, cost, or data-handling questions:
Scope limits and accepted tradeoffs:
Evidence links and review date:
First evaluation and expected signal:
Decision: evaluate / adopt / defer / reject
Owner and revisit condition:
```

For example, a Python service may use Ruff for selected lint rules and mypy for
type consistency. The note should name both jobs, the checked package, and any
missing stubs. It should not turn the two tools' finding categories into a claim
of complete coverage.

Check unresolved prerequisites before adopting a workflow. A builder candidate
means its reviewed conditions fit the supplied description; it does not mean the
tool ran or that every library and version is compatible. Link the exact profile
notes that support the decision.

## Move from a choice to evidence

Run a small check with a known expected signal, then preserve a
[run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Keep the selection rationale here and the actual
commands, reports, and results in that record. The
[Python linting and types recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) shows how complementary
tools can share inputs while keeping their findings separate.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/choosing-and-recording-tools/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/choosing-and-recording-tools.json).

documents.title: Run repeatable CI checks
documents.description: Reuse a local analysis recipe in CI while retaining findings, failure logs, and an explicit gate.
documents.markdown:
# Run repeatable CI checks

**Make the local check reproducible before making it a required CI job.** This guide uses the [Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/), its pinned environment, and the shared [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). CI-provider setup remains illustrative until tested in your own pipeline.

## Prepare the job

1. Check out the intended revision. Record the commit and any local changes; choose a fresh report directory for this run.
2. Create the recipe's Python environment and install its pinned requirements. Retain installation logs if setup fails.
3. Use the checked-in `pyproject.toml` and explicit input path. The recipe invokes Ruff without automatic fixes and keeps mypy's report separate. Record the tool versions and configuration hashes.
4. Decide the gate before running. The policy below requires both checks to complete without findings; it does not silently accept new suppressions or baselines.

From the recipe directory, run the corrected fixture using its existing runner:

```powershell
.venv/Scripts/python run_checks.py good --output reports/ci
```

Use `.venv/bin/python` on Linux or macOS. This selects the recipe environment
without relying on shell activation.

This is a smoke check of the recipe, not a check of your whole application. When adapting it, select your own source scope and configuration explicitly and retain a known faulty/corrected pair that shows the intended checks are active.

The runner returns `0` when both checks complete cleanly, `1` for completed checks with findings, and `2` for failed or incomplete analysis. It runs both tools and preserves their separate reports in the output directory.

## Interpret the result before applying the gate

Use the states in [Review analysis findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/#check-the-run). A required check passes only when its intended scope is `completed-no-findings` and its evidence is present.

| Result                                           | Gate action in this example                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Both checks completed without findings           | Pass. Retain both reports and the run record.                                     |
| At least one check completed with findings       | Fail the gate and link to the report for review.                                  |
| Setup, execution, or report validation failed    | Fail the gate as an analysis failure; retain logs.                                |
| Required check skipped, cancelled, or incomplete | Do not report a pass. Preserve the reason and rerun or resolve the missing scope. |

For non-fixing `ruff check`, status `0` indicates no violations, `1` indicates violations, and `2` indicates abnormal termination. Fix and exit-control flags change this interpretation; the recipe uses `--no-fix` and does not use `--exit-zero`. [Ruff's return-code contract](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/#exit-codes).

The pinned mypy runner also separates diagnostic results from blocking errors. Its 1.18.2 implementation uses status `1` for ordinary diagnostic errors and `2` for blocking failures, with `0` for no errors. Read the report and completion summary as well as the code; a syntax error can prevent later checks. [mypy 1.18.2 command implementation](https://github.com/python/mypy/blob/v1.18.2/mypy/main.py).

These codes are tool-specific. Do not map every nonzero status from another analyzer to "findings," or treat a missing report as an empty one.

## Retain evidence even when a check fails

Configure your CI provider to preserve the report directory after failed analysis as well as successful analysis. Keep stdout/stderr, the runner's record, tool versions, target/configuration hashes, and the provider's job status. Retain the setup log when the runner never starts. A cancelled job may leave partial artifacts; label them as partial.

Keep the analyzer's status when invoking an artifact-upload step. A successful upload must not replace a failed check's result, and a failed upload means the expected evidence is missing. Choose artifact retention and access according to the report's contents; diagnostic paths and code excerpts can reveal project information.

## Adopt a policy deliberately

This recipe blocks on every diagnostic. For an existing project, review the rule set and scope, then decide whether existing findings need a tracked remediation period. Do not regenerate baselines to force a pass.

Review an exception with its rule, location, evidence, owner, and expiry or review condition. Keep a suppression or baseline change distinct from a repair, and compare runs after intended version or rule changes. [Review analysis findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/#investigate-and-decide) provides the shared procedure.

The [CI/CD research note](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-workflow/) describes a separate SonarQube/GitLab integration study. This guide supplies result-handling steps for the Python recipe; it does not implement that study's connector.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/ci-checks.json).

documents.title: Data and AI access
documents.description: Download ToolWiki data or give an agent direct access through ordinary URLs.
documents.markdown:
# Data and AI access

Read ToolWiki from the website, a script, or an agent that can fetch URLs. The
files below are generated with the site. No account, API key, repository clone,
or local server is needed.

On tool profiles and articles, use **Copy as Markdown** to copy the text with
sources, evidence status, and its content revision. **Read Markdown** and
**View JSON** open the files directly and work without JavaScript. If clipboard
access is unavailable, the copy button provides selectable text instead.

## Choose what to download

- **Tool catalog:** Filter a compact list of tool names, aliases, languages,
  inputs, findings, costs, and reviewed workflow platforms. Follow each record's
  links for complete requirements and workflow details.
- **Document index:** Find tool profiles, guides, concepts, and research notes by
  title and description. Each entry links to its Markdown and JSON record.
- **Markdown:** Read a profile or workflow as text, including tool compatibility,
  cost conditions, sources, and evidence status.
- **JSON record:** Read the same document with structured tool metadata, section
  offsets, citations, and its content revision.
- **Complete snapshot:** Download every document and tool record in one JSON
  file for local search, comparison, or offline use.
- **Manifest:** Find the current snapshot, its revision, and file checksums.

Start with the [tool catalog](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/catalog.json) or
[document index](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/index.json), or try the
[Ruff Markdown profile](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/tools/ruff.md) and
[Ruff JSON record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/tools/ruff.json).
The [data format reference](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/data-reference/) explains fields, allowed values,
and evidence semantics. Download the [JSON Schema index](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/index.json)
and [filter vocabulary](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/vocabulary.json) for programmatic use.

## Give an agent access

Copy this request into an agent that can fetch public URLs, replacing the task
in the first sentence:

```text
Use ToolWiki to find tools for Python linting and type checks.
Start at https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/llms.txt and follow its links to
the document index and relevant JSON or Markdown records. Read requirements,
limitations, and evidence scope before recommending a tool. Inspect my existing
project configuration before proposing commands or configuration changes.
Cite the ToolWiki page URLs and the revisions from the JSON records you use.
```

If the agent cannot fetch URLs, download the relevant records and attach them
using that agent's file input. The optional [local MCP connection](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/using-with-agents/)
offers named search and comparison tools for clients that support it.

## Fetch documents from a script

This Python 3 example uses only the standard library. It reads the index and
prints Markdown URLs for documents mentioning Python in their title or description:

```python
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen

base = "https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/"
with urlopen(base + "index.json", timeout=30) as response:
    index = json.load(response)

for document in index["documents"]:
    summary = document["title"] + " " + document["description"]
    if "python" in summary.lower():
        print(document["id"], base + document["markdown"])
```

These are static files. A URL query such as `?language=Python` does not filter
the JSON response; your script or agent filters downloaded data locally.

To find Python source tools, fetch `catalog.json` instead and filter its `tools`
array where `languages` includes `Python` and `inputTypes` includes `Source code`.
Retain `languageNote`, `findingNote`, and `costNote` when presenting matches.
`reviewedHostPlatforms` and `reviewedTargetPlatforms` are unions of the tool's
reviewed workflows, not exhaustive support lists or guarantees for every mode.
An empty list means no platform is listed there; it does not mean unsupported.

## Download selections and recommendations

In the catalog, **Download these results** saves the current filtered results
in their displayed order as JSON or CSV. JSON includes the filters, source URL,
snapshot revision, and tool records. CSV keeps the tool fields and scope notes;
lists use `/` between values and cells that could be spreadsheet formulas are
prefixed with an apostrophe. Use JSON when you need the exact structured values.

On **Compare tools**, choose two or three tools and use **Download comparison
(Markdown)**. It includes the comparison fields, related explanations, sources,
and evidence status, including details in the collapsed table.

In **Find tools for your system**, download recommendations as Markdown or JSON
from **Tool candidates**. Reports include your current description and notes,
selected tools, candidate and blocked matches, unanswered questions, gaps, and
source revisions. They do not establish that any check has run. **Export system**
still saves just the description for later import; recommendation reports are a
separate format for reading and sharing. Files are created in your browser.

## Keep a consistent copy

Read the [manifest](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/manifest.json), then fetch the path in
`snapshot.path` relative to the manifest URL. Check its byte count and SHA-256
against `snapshot.bytes` and `snapshot.sha256`. Keep that validated snapshot
for the whole task. A deployment can replace individual files between requests;
if a snapshot disappears during an update, fetch the manifest again and retry.
The [change history](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/changes/) and [JSON change feed](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/history/index.json)
list selected retained snapshots with byte counts and SHA-256 checksums. A snapshot
listed there remains available at its revision URL. The archive does not include
every deployment; save unlisted snapshots when reproducibility matters. A capture
date records when a snapshot was retained, not when its documentation was reviewed.

A revision identifies content, not a review date. Documentation review and
recorded execution are separate. `not-recorded` means no structured execution
record is supplied; it does not mean a check failed or an example was never run.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/data-access/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/data-access.json).
