documents.title: Data format reference
documents.description: Static JSON schemas, field meanings, filter values, revisions, and evidence semantics.
documents.markdown:
# Data format reference

Start with [Data and AI access](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/data-access/) for downloads and a fetch example.
All paths below are relative to the
[knowledge manifest](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/manifest.json) at `/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/`.
Files use UTF-8. No request parameters or authentication are required.

## Files and schemas

The [schema index](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/index.json) lists the downloadable
schemas and their stable identifiers. They use JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 and are
generated from the schemas used by the site. The
[vocabulary file](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/vocabulary.json) lists the current filter
values and system-builder choices.

| Data                           | JSON Schema                                                                                             | Purpose                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `manifest.json`                | [Manifest](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/manifest.schema.json)               | Snapshot pointer and file checksums.                     |
| `index.json`                   | [Document index](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/index.schema.json)            | All published documents and links to their records.      |
| `documents/{id}.json`          | [Document](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/document.schema.json)               | One complete document, including its Markdown.           |
| The document's `tool` property | [Tool metadata](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/tool.schema.json)              | Tool capabilities, costs, scope, and reviewed workflows. |
| `snapshots/{revision}.json`    | [Snapshot](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/snapshot.schema.json)               | All records from one revision.                           |
| `catalog.json`                 | [Catalog](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/catalog.schema.json)                 | Compact tool discovery records.                          |
| **Export system** download     | [System profile](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/system-profile.schema.json)   | Editable components, connections, and preferences.       |
| Filtered catalog JSON download | [Catalog results](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/catalog-results.schema.json) | Filter state and ordered tool records.                   |
| Recommendation JSON download   | [Recommendations](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/schemas/recommendations.schema.json) | Input, matches, gaps, selections, and cited tools.       |

`documents/{id}.md` is the document's Markdown as a standalone text file. Its
canonical page URL and JSON-record link identify the source. **Copy as Markdown**
adds the content revision from that JSON record. Comparison and recommendation
Markdown downloads are readable reports; their structured equivalents are the
tool records and recommendation JSON respectively.

## Document fields

| Field                  | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                   | Stable document identifier such as `tools/ruff` or `guides/python-checks`.                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `kind`                 | `tool`, `guide`, `concept`, `research`, or `page`.                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `title`, `description` | Display name and concise description.                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `url`                  | Canonical website URL to cite.                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `revision`             | SHA-256 content identity for this record, not a date or tool version.                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `markdown`             | Complete article text, with tool decision facts, compatibility, editions, sources, and evidence where applicable. Relative Markdown links become absolute; code blocks remain unchanged.                                                      |
| `sections`             | Heading `id`, `title`, `depth`, `start`, and `end`. Offsets are zero-based UTF-16 code units into `markdown`, with an exclusive end. A section includes child headings. IDs match website anchors, including custom metadata-section anchors. |
| `sources`              | Objects with a `label` and absolute `url`. Includes tool references and links found in the exported text; not every link is independent evidence.                                                                                             |
| `evidence`             | Documentation-review date and separately recorded execution evidence. See below.                                                                                                                                                              |
| `tool`                 | Present only for tool profiles. Validated metadata used by the catalog, comparisons, and system builder.                                                                                                                                      |

The index replaces `markdown` text with a relative Markdown file path, adds a
`record` path to JSON, and omits `tool`, `sources`, and section offsets. It keeps
each document's identity, description, evidence, and revision. Its top-level
`revision` is the snapshot revision.

## Catalog and tool fields

The catalog's `tools` array contains discovery records, not full workflow
definitions. Fetch a record through its `record` path before choosing a workflow.
The catalog's top-level `revision` identifies the snapshot; each tool's
`revision` identifies that document. Paths are relative to the manifest.

| Field or group                                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`, `title`, `description`, `url`, `revision`, `evidence` | Same identity and evidence as the document record.                                                                                          |
| `record`, `markdown`                                        | Relative JSON and Markdown paths.                                                                                                           |
| `aliases`, `searchTerms`                                    | Alternate names and documented search phrases.                                                                                              |
| `modes`, `techniques`                                       | Static/dynamic categories and analysis methods.                                                                                             |
| `inputTypes`, `targets`                                     | Materials examined and software context. A language tag alone does not imply source-code analysis.                                          |
| `languages`, `languageNote`                                 | Languages or ecosystems and qualifications on that support.                                                                                 |
| `findings`, `findingNote`                                   | Finding categories and the conditions under which checks apply. Matching labels do not imply equal detection or coverage.                   |
| `cost`, `costNote`, `licenseCategory`                       | Continuing cost categories, eligibility or edition conditions, and license class. Trials are not free editions.                             |
| `environment`, `scope`                                      | Where the tool runs and the edition, component, or verified version described.                                                              |
| `reviewedHostPlatforms`, `reviewedTargetPlatforms`          | Catalog-only unions of reviewed workflow platforms. They are not exhaustive support lists and do not establish support for every tool mode. |

The full `tool` object additionally supplies `website`, `license`, `verified`,
`setup`, optional `cardRequirement`, optional `decision` (`useWhen`, `result`,
`limit`), optional `editionGroup`, and `analysisWorkflows`. It uses `verified`
for the same date exposed as `evidence.documentationReviewedOn` in the record.
The [authoring field guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/editing/#metadata-fields) explains every tool field.

Each workflow has its own inputs, findings, requirements, platform lists,
sources, and caveat. Keep alternative workflows separate; do not combine their
requirements or capabilities. See [workflow fields](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/editing/#add-a-builder-workflow)
for the complete dictionary.

## Allowed values and unknowns

Use `vocabulary.json` rather than guessing spelling or capitalization. Its
`catalog` object maps filter names to current values: `mode`, `input`,
`language`, `finding`, `technique`, `license`, and `cost`. For example,
`input: "Source code"` maps to membership in a tool's `inputTypes` array.
`filterSentinels` describes the UI's empty selection, `any-free` cost preference,
and sort values; these are not tool metadata tags.

In system profiles, `unknown` is an unanswered access question, while `no` is an
explicit negative answer. Empty platform choices mean unspecified. An empty
workflow platform list does not mean unsupported; explicit `excludedHosts` and
`excludedTargets` carry exclusions. When `inputsComplete` is false, an omitted
input remains unconfirmed. When true, omitted inputs are unavailable.

`candidate` means the recorded requirements match the supplied description.
`details` means more information is needed. `blocked` means at least one stated
requirement is unmet. `gap` means no reviewed workflow matched that subject;
it does not prove no suitable tool exists. An undescribed subject has
`needsDescription: true` and may have no gap entry. None of these statuses
establishes execution, measured coverage, or permission to run a check.

## Evidence and freshness

| Field                              | Meaning                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `evidence.documentationReviewedOn` | `YYYY-MM-DD` documentation review date, or `null` when no structured date is supplied. It is not the build date. |
| `evidence.execution.status`        | `recorded` or `not-recorded`.                                                                                    |
| `evidence.execution.scope`         | The tested environment and limits, or an explanation of missing structured evidence.                             |
| `evidence.execution.sources`       | URLs to execution records. A recorded status requires at least one source.                                       |

`not-recorded` does not mean an example failed or has never run. Read the scope
and article qualifications. A recorded execution applies to its stated
environment and version; it is separate from a current documentation review.

## Revisions and validation

`version` is the format version. `revision` in the manifest, index, catalog, and
snapshot identifies the snapshot content. Reports and vocabulary call that value
`snapshotRevision` to distinguish it from document revisions. A document hash is
computed from its JSON without `revision`, sorting object keys recursively,
preserving array order, using two-space indentation and one final newline. The
snapshot hash uses the same rule over its payload.

Manifest SHA-256 values cover exact UTF-8 file bytes. Verify both hashes and byte
counts when retaining a snapshot. Hashes detect changed bytes and mixed files;
they do not authenticate the publisher. Additional downloadable files can appear
in version 1, so follow the manifest inventory instead of hardcoding its length.

Schemas validate structure, required fields, types, enum values, and bounds.
They do not recompute hashes or fully express cross-field rules. The site also
checks unique IDs, valid connection endpoints, unique profile list values,
workflow findings and sources against their tool profile, and workflow-specific
input requirements. Saved system files additionally have a 1 MiB UTF-8 limit.
Section offsets must be ordered and within the Markdown string. Reports must
refer to their included tool and subject IDs and retain the results of the
matching rules. Do not treat structural schema validation as evidence of factual
correctness or compatibility.

To validate a downloaded Ruff record, first save the document schema as
`document.schema.json` and the record as `ruff.json` in the same directory.
With Python 3 and the `jsonschema` package installed, run:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator

schema = json.loads(Path("document.schema.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
record = json.loads(Path("ruff.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
Draft202012Validator.check_schema(schema)
Draft202012Validator(schema).validate(record)
print("Document structure is valid.")
```

## Downloaded report fields

Filtered catalog JSON includes `version`, `kind: "catalog-results"`,
`snapshotRevision`, `sourceUrl`, `knowledgeBase`, `filters`, `count`, and ordered
`tools`. Resolve record paths against `knowledgeBase`. CSV flattens these tool
fields; lists use `/`, standard CSV quoting preserves commas and newlines, and
an apostrophe protects formula-like cells. JSON preserves the original strings.

Recommendation JSON includes `version`, `kind: "recommendations"`,
`snapshotRevision`, `sourceUrl`, `limitation`, `profile`, `selectedToolIds`,
`results`, and the referenced `tools`. The input profile contains components,
connections, notes, and preferences; the
[system authoring guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/editing/#use-and-save-a-system) explains import and
recovery. `selectedToolIds` records a comparison shortlist, not executed checks.

`results.subjects` contains each included part's name, description status, and
grouped nonblocked candidates. `results.matches` contains all applicable
workflow evaluations, including blocked ones. Each match names its tool,
workflow, subject, findings, status, `reasons`, `unresolved` questions, and
`blocked` requirements. `questions` gives a field, message, and whether an answer
or compatibility verification is needed. `goalIds` classifies findings and does
not filter matches. `results.gaps` summarizes each described part's match status
and reasons. The referenced tool records retain setup, scope, costs, workflows,
and a `citation` containing the document URL, revision, and evidence.

## Change feed and retained snapshots

[`history/index.json`](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/history/index.json) has `version: 1`, `site`,
`currentRevision`, a retention explanation, and `entries` in reverse capture order.
Resolve each entry's snapshot `path` against `site`, not against the feed URL.
The [readable history](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/changes/) and [Markdown feed](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/history/changes.md)
present the same comparison.

Each entry has a `revision`, `label`, `capturedOn`, `current`, `documentCount`,
`path`, `sha256`, and `bytes`. A current build that has not been archived has
`capturedOn: null`. Retained capture dates do not imply publication dates or
new documentation reviews. Only listed archives are retained across deployments.

`previousRevision` identifies the preceding selected snapshot; `changes` is
null for the archive baseline. Later entries have `changes.added`,
`changes.changed`, and `changes.removed` arrays. Records contain document `id`,
`title`, canonical `url`, and content `revision`; changed records also include
`previousRevision`. Changes are content-hash differences, so formatting and
export improvements can change many records without changing their tool claims.
An empty array means no difference of that kind between these selected snapshots.

To retrieve a removed record, download the entry named by `previousRevision`,
validate its bytes and checksum, and select the ID from its `documents` array.
The removed record's canonical page URL may no longer exist. The current manifest
continues to inventory only the current export; archive checksums live in the feed.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/data-reference/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/data-reference.json).

- **Documentation reviewed:** Not recorded
- **Execution evidence:** not-recorded
- **Execution scope:** No structured execution record for this document. Read the text for illustrative examples and limitations.

Documentation review is separate from execution evidence. A recorded execution applies only to its stated environment and scope; not-recorded means no structured execution record is supplied.

execution.scope: No structured execution record for this document. Read the text for illustrative examples and limitations.

documents.title: Add or update a tool
documents.description: Maintain one Markdown file per tool and let the catalog update itself.
documents.markdown:
# Add or update a tool

Each tool has one Markdown file in `src/content/docs/tools/`. Its metadata supplies the catalog filters, decision summary, and comparison. The body explains how to use and interpret the tool.

Start with the reader's decision and first useful result. Put detailed compatibility, editions, and sources after the practical explanation. Keep one clear limitation beside the claim it qualifies instead of repeating it throughout the page.

## Update an existing entry

1. Open its file, or use **Edit page** at the bottom of the tool's page to edit on GitHub.
2. Update the facts and notes against primary documentation.
3. Update `verified` only when you have checked the sources. Record an exact version in `scope` when the claim depends on one.
4. Review the live preview and run the checks described in the repository README.

Record the review's scope and file digest in the repository's
[current review ledger](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/audits/review-status).
Historical audit records stay unchanged. Use a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/) for
actual tool execution; a documentation review and an example run are different evidence.

## Add an entry

Only admit a tool when its primary documentation supports a useful, scoped profile. A directory listing or product landing page can identify a candidate, but is not sufficient evidence by itself.

Before adding it, verify:

- What it examines, which languages or formats it covers, and which component or edition is described.
- How to install or access it, prepare its inputs, and follow a documented first-use workflow.
- What its findings mean, with a rule reference, example report, or explanation of result types.
- The material limits, such as required instrumentation, incomplete language support, exploration bounds, or external data dependencies.
- Its license and usage terms, including restrictions on required solvers or services.

Cite official guides and license evidence, and record the review date. A detailed official repository guide can qualify; link counts alone do not establish quality. Keep unverifiable candidates in research notes and limit entries to documented capabilities.

1. Copy a similar tool file into the same folder using a lowercase, hyphenated filename ending in `.md`.
2. Replace its title, description, metadata, sources, and notes.
3. Use existing tag spellings where possible. New tags in filterable fields automatically appear in the filters.

The entry automatically appears in the catalog, the matching analysis section, and the published site's search index. The sidebar provides routes into the catalog rather than repeating the full tool list. A tool can use both `Static` and `Dynamic` in `modes`.

## Metadata fields

| Field                    | What to record                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`, `description`   | Tool name and a short factual description.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `tool.cardRequirement`   | Optional short prerequisite that changes the reader's choice, shown on the catalog card. State it explicitly; do not infer product-wide requirements from the subset of reviewed builder workflows.                                                                                                               |
| `tool.decision`          | Optional object with `useWhen`, `result`, and `limit`. Describe the task, the result and its meaning, and the main limit. These appear in the profile and comparison. When supplied, include a `## First try` section with prerequisites, an example or official tutorial, expected result, and execution status. |
| `tool.aliases`           | Optional list of common names or abbreviations, such as `[ASan, Address Sanitizer]`. Used for catalog matching and shown on the tool page. Defaults to an empty list.                                                                                                                                             |
| `tool.searchTerms`       | Optional list of additional, source-supported capability phrases, such as `[buffer overflow]`. Used only by catalog search. Defaults to an empty list.                                                                                                                                                            |
| `tool.modes`             | A list containing `Static`, `Dynamic`, or both.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `tool.inputTypes`        | One or more of `Source code`, `Binaries`, `Dependency metadata`, `Container images`, `Configuration files`, `Running applications`, `Callable code`, `Executable models`, or `Execution traces`. Drives the Input type filter.                                                                                    |
| `tool.findings`          | Selected finding categories, such as `Memory safety`, `Injection risks`, `Type errors`, or `Specification violations`. Drives What can it find?                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `tool.findingNote`       | Explain whether the findings need selected rules, manual investigation, assertions, instrumentation, or user-supplied specifications.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `tool.environment`       | Where the analyzer runs, including OS, runtime, container/WSL routes, and documented compatibility limits. Distinguish host from target.                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `tool.setup`             | Build, dependency, harness, annotation, and other preparation requirements.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `tool.techniques`        | Analysis methods such as `SAST`, `DAST`, or `Coverage-guided fuzzing`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `tool.languages`         | Languages or ecosystems in this entry's verified scope.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `tool.languageNote`      | Coverage limits, incomplete lists, or language-independent behavior.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `tool.targets`           | Software context such as `Firmware`, `Notebooks`, or `HTTP APIs`. Searchable in the catalog and shown as Context in the tool notes, with exact Input type duplicates omitted. This is not a separate filter.                                                                                                      |
| `tool.licenseCategory`   | `Open source`, `Source available`, or `Proprietary`, for the component this entry covers. Source access alone does not establish open-source licensing.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `tool.license`           | Specific terms and edition caveats.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `tool.cost`              | A list containing `Free`, `Free with limits`, and/or `Paid`. Multiple values represent different usage entitlements or plans for this entry.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `tool.costNote`          | Explain free-use eligibility, usage limits, and any paid alternatives. Do not count a time-limited trial as a free edition.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `tool.editionGroup`      | Optional shared comparison: `codeql`, `sonarqube`, `semgrep`, `burp`, `cppcheck`, `pvs-studio`, `phpstan`, `coverity`, or `polyspace`. The table lives in `src/data/editions.mjs`.                                                                                                                                |
| `tool.website`           | The official product or project URL.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `tool.verified`          | A quoted date such as `'2026-09-21'`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `tool.scope`             | Product edition, component, and any verified version.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `tool.sources`           | A list of `label` and `url` pairs for primary references.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `tool.analysisWorkflows` | Optional scoped workflows for the analysis suite builder. Defaults to an empty list; see below.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

## Add a builder workflow

The [analysis suite builder](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/analysis-suite/) matches individual workflows rather than combining a tool's catalog tags. A tool without a reviewed workflow remains in the catalog but does not generate builder recommendations. Historical matching decisions are in `audits/system-builder/README.md`; later additions have scoped records under `audits/remaining-work/`.

1. Check the entry's primary documentation for one concrete workflow, including its language, input, findings, and preparation requirements.
2. Add an item to `tool.analysisWorkflows`. Keep alternative inputs, plugins, editions, and analysis modes separate whenever their requirements or findings differ.
3. Reference evidence URLs already listed in `tool.sources`. Retain the entry's verification date unless you have rechecked its documented claims.
4. Try a matching system, an incomplete description, and an incompatible system in the builder. Run `pnpm verify` to check metadata, matching, and generated pages.

This example describes a hypothetical Python source workflow; adapt its finding and evidence to the actual tool:

```yaml
analysisWorkflows:
  - id: python-source
    label: Python source checks
    subject: component
    inputs: [Source code]
    languageScope: source
    languages: [Python]
    findings: [Logic errors]
    caveat: Selected rules only; verify supported syntax and configuration.
    sources:
      - https://example.org/official-tool-documentation
```

The fields above are required, except `languages` may be empty for `languageScope: independent`. These additional fields default to empty lists:

| Field                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `interfaces`, `transports`         | Explicit application interfaces and transports for a connection workflow. Connections require at least one interface. TCP support alone is not MQTT or HTTP support. |
| `definitions`                      | Accepted API definitions: `OpenAPI` or `GraphQL schema`. A definition and a reachable test service are separate requirements.                                        |
| `binaryFormats`                    | Accepted binary artifacts, such as `Native executable`, `JVM bytecode`, or `LLVM bitcode`. Required when a component workflow takes `Binaries`.                      |
| `technologies`                     | Additional required technologies, such as `Ruby on Rails` or `MATLAB`. At least one must be confirmed.                                                               |
| `requires`                         | Required access: `rebuild`, `instrument`, `harness`, and/or `testInstance`. Unknown answers request detail; an explicit No blocks the workflow.                      |
| `hostPlatforms`, `targetPlatforms` | Documented OS examples for the analysis host and target. Unlisted platforms need confirmation; these lists are not exhaustive exclusions.                            |
| `excludedHosts`, `excludedTargets` | Explicit, evidence-backed incompatibilities. Do not infer them from a platform missing from an example list.                                                         |

`subject` is `component` or `connection`. `languageScope` is `source`, `ecosystem`, `independent`, `model`, or `configuration`. Ecosystem languages describe dependency support. Ecosystem, configuration, and model workflows also inspect selected technologies. All listed `inputs` are required together; use separate workflows for alternatives. An instrumented-build workflow can require source even when the catalog input is the executable it eventually checks.

Workflow findings must be supported by the entry and that particular workflow. Do not give every language all of a product's aggregate capabilities. Record rule, version, plugin, solver, and architecture qualifications in `caveat`; results also display setup, environment, scope, and cost notes. Candidate status means recorded requirements matched, not that all compatibility details or findings were demonstrated.

Keep controlled choices in `src/lib/system-schema.mjs` consistent with metadata. Add focused tests for new matching distinctions. Preserve subject, finding, tool, and workflow relationships so a future coverage view can use the same evidence. Finding categories are derived from matched workflows; users do not need to select investigation goals.

## Use and save a system

Add component cards, select their languages and available material, then optionally describe connections. Language and ecosystem choices open by default and can be collapsed. All matching candidates appear automatically from the system description, and each card explains what it can help find. There is no shortlist limit or investigation-goal selection. Unchecked material is unknown until you select **Only these materials are available**. Names, component types, deployment context, and free-text notes describe the system; they are not searched for inferred capabilities.

The optional **Match status by component and connection** summary reports candidates, missing information, unmet requirements, or no reviewed catalog match for each described part. Blank parts prompt for a description instead of suggesting every tool. At least one selected language, ecosystem, material, or interface must support each suggested workflow. An absent match does not establish that no suitable tool exists, and a candidate does not represent completed testing or full coverage.

Existing version 1 system files remain supported. Their legacy `goals` fields are optional and no longer filter recommendations, including after restoring browser storage or importing a file.

The latest description saves in this browser. **Export system** downloads a version 1 JSON file; **Import system** validates it before replacing the description and recomputes candidates from the current catalog. System files support up to 1 MiB, 50 components, and 100 connections. The imported description must also fit the byte limit when formatted for saving; a compact file can expand during that preparation. Rejected imports preserve the current description, selection, undo state, and stored data. **Undo removal or import** restores the most recently removed part and its incident connections while preserving later edits. Undoing an import restores the entire description from before that import.

If edits exceed the byte limit, the current description stays in memory and the previous valid saved copy is kept. Reduce notes, selected languages, or system parts before saving or exporting. An oversized export produces no download. For a description within the limit, export before leaving if browser storage is unavailable.

If existing saved data cannot be read, automatic saving pauses to protect it. **Download recovery data** keeps the raw saved copy; this file may need correction or reduction before it can be imported and is not a normal system export. Importing a valid description or using Undo does not remove that protection. Only a confirmed **Replace saved system** action writes the current description over the protected copy, and protection remains if validation or the write fails. Downloading recovery data alone does not authorize replacement.

If storage itself could not be read, use **Retry reading saved data**. The retry keeps current in-memory edits. Any existing saved copy found by the retry remains protected until explicitly replaced; an absent saved copy allows normal saving to resume. Clearing site data removes the local copy. Comparison selections are temporary and open the comparison page in a new tab. System exports contain descriptions and preferences, not tool results.

## Make tools easy to find

Catalog search ranks exact names and aliases first, followed by names, capability tags, and descriptions. With no query, Best match lists entries alphabetically. Readers can still choose an explicit name or verification-date sort.

Add aliases for the exact entry's name, not for a different edition or predecessor. Keep capability phrases tied to the sources and scope already documented on the page. For example, a race detector can have `race conditions` as a search phrase without implying that it detects all concurrency failures.

Search understands common language spellings such as `cpp`, `C sharp`, `js`, and `golang`. It keeps C, C++, C#, Java, and JavaScript distinct. Search terms must all match; spelling suggestions appear separately when there are no results and retain the current filters. This is keyword search, not a natural-language question-answering system.

The catalog does not search the full article, platform caveats, or cost notes. Those can mention unsupported features or other editions. Use **Search tools, capabilities, and all pages** to search the full notes and guides. Aliases shown on tool pages are also indexed there when the site is built.

Check the official name, each alias, a capability phrase, and a relevant combination of filters after editing an entry. Ensure a free-edition search cannot inherit a paid edition's capabilities. Search and filter choices remain in category links and bookmark URLs.

## Keep claims scoped

Record what the analyzer examines in `inputTypes`, rather than the language used to implement the analyzer. Binary inspection is `Binaries`; manifest or SBOM matching is `Dependency metadata`. Use multiple values when separate documented workflows accept different inputs. Analysis mode remains separate: a binary can be inspected statically or executed under a dynamic checker.

Explain native executable versus JVM bytecode in the notes, and say whether a binary must be rebuilt with instrumentation. `Container images` describes an image artifact inspected at rest, not a running container. Trace monitoring remains dynamic analysis even when a monitor reads saved execution data offline.

Use `Configuration files` for infrastructure definitions such as Terraform, Dockerfiles, or Kubernetes manifests. Configuration analysis does not establish support for general application-source analysis; do not tag a dependency/configuration scanner as `Source code` merely because it scans a repository.

Language tags on a dependency scanner describe package ecosystems. They do not imply source-level analysis. Do not copy a bundled utility's broader language list into an entry for a different capability, such as PMD rules versus CPD duplicate detection.

Finding categories are selected capabilities, not exhaustive coverage claims. Do not claim that a fuzzer supplies a property checker just because an assertion can be placed in its harness. Explain that dependency in `findingNote`. The comparison page reads these same fields automatically, so keep them useful without relying on the surrounding article.

Cost and license type answer different questions. Proprietary software can be free to use. "Free with limits" means a continuing free option with eligibility or usage conditions, rather than a trial.

Keep separately filterable entries when editions have different language or analysis capabilities. For example, do not label the paid edition's C++ analyzer as free just because a free edition of the product exists. Update the shared edition comparison when a product changes its free plan or paid features.

Separate documentation review from hands-on experience. Record your test environment and versions if you add evaluation results. Avoid treating an unlisted language as unsupported when an entry only includes selected examples.

For worked examples, state the prerequisites, input, command or configuration, and how to interpret the result. Label examples that have not been run; do not present expected output as a captured result. Keep simulator, compiler, plugin, and license requirements explicit.

Use ordinary Markdown headings beginning at level two (`##`); the site supplies the page title. Relative links should point to the rendered page path and end with a slash.

## Add research notes and connections

Research notes live in `src/content/docs/research/`. Copy the structure of a similar note: the practical question, study or proposal, findings, limitations, suggested application, and a full paper citation with a source link. Keep your suggested workflow separate from observations actually reported in the paper.

Write research notes from Zach's perspective: use "I" for personal discussion and recommendations, and "we" for work with coauthors. Follow the papers' terminology and keep headings short and descriptive, such as Methods, Findings, and Limitations. Preserve uncertainty and the distinction between proposed methods and evaluated results.

Add a new note to the Research notes group in `astro.config.mjs` and link it from the research overview. Record the publication year separately from a later preprint-upload date. Prefer an author copy or publisher source and point readers to the relevant sections. Do not treat a thesis chapter and its corresponding conference paper as independent evidence.

On a relevant tool page, add a `## Related research` section in the Markdown body. Link to both the local note and the paper, and explain the connection: used in the study, discussed in a proposal, or related through a product family. A mention alone does not establish that the tool was evaluated.

Keep current edition coverage and historical study configurations distinct. Record missing configuration details rather than assigning old findings to a current paid or free edition. Updating a research connection alone does not update the tool's documentation-verification date.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/editing/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/editing.json).

- **Documentation reviewed:** Not recorded
- **Execution evidence:** not-recorded
- **Execution scope:** No structured execution record for this document. Read the text for illustrative examples and limitations.

Documentation review is separate from execution evidence. A recorded execution applies only to its stated environment and scope; not-recorded means no structured execution record is supplied.

documents.markdown:
# Check execution and data boundaries

**Choose a workflow before deciding whether a tool fits a restricted environment.** Local analysis can still fetch rules, query a service, or submit results. License and price do not establish where data goes.

This review covers official documentation available on November 6, 2026. It is not a network-traffic test. OSV guidance is for V2; the cited Grype configuration reference is generated for 0.119.0. Semgrep and Trivy links track their current documentation. Check your installed release before applying the options below.

## Semgrep CE with local rules

[Semgrep CE](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-ce/) runs rules on local files. A standalone `semgrep scan` does not require a Semgrep account. Rule files can be local, URLs, or Registry entries; remote rules must be retrieved. Version checking is a separate network operation, controlled by `--disable-version-check`. [CLI reference](https://docs.semgrep.dev/cli-reference).

The default metrics policy enables metrics for Registry rules or logged-in use. Local rules alone do not enable them. `--metrics off` controls metrics, not rule retrieval, version checks, or explicit platform reporting. Record the rule source and revision along with the CLI version. [Metrics policy](https://docs.semgrep.dev/metrics).

For disconnected use, prepare the engine and compatible local rules first, choose local output files, and review the installed CLI's network-related options. This page does not validate a complete offline setup.

## Semgrep Code with platform reporting

For [Semgrep Code](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-code/) in your CI, scanning runs on the configured runner. The connected workflow requires a platform account and token, obtains its configuration, and sends findings to the AppSec Platform. Account and repository permissions are part of that setup. [CI deployment guide](https://docs.semgrep.dev/deployment/add-semgrep-to-ci).

Metrics and findings are different transmissions: the metrics policy describes aggregate usage data, while logged-in `semgrep ci` also sends finding and repository information for the dashboard. Turning metrics off does not disconnect that workflow. [Metrics policy](https://docs.semgrep.dev/metrics).

Managed Scans run on Semgrep's infrastructure: the service clones the selected repository, scans it, then removes the clone. [Managed Scans lifecycle](https://docs.semgrep.dev/deployment/managed-scanning/overview#life-cycle-of-a-managed-scan).

Pro-engine installation, platform policies, and entitlement need review for the chosen release. A connected workflow is not established as offline-capable by saving a rule file. AI features and other Semgrep products are outside this comparison.

## OSV-Scanner dependency matching

[OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/) extracts package information locally, then normally queries OSV.dev for vulnerability matching. The CLI workflow does not require a hosted dashboard account. Online matching sends the package-query information to the service; selected dependency-resolution features can make further requests. A local output file is separate from any report publishing you configure. [V2 usage](https://google.github.io/osv-scanner/usage/).

Full `--offline` mode uses previously downloaded ecosystem databases. The docs distinguish it from `--offline-vulnerabilities`, which only changes vulnerability matching and allows other features to use the network. Adding `--download-offline-databases` deliberately enables database retrieval. Prepare the required ecosystems and record their dates; missing databases are an error, and old data cannot include newer advisories. [Offline modes](https://google.github.io/osv-scanner/usage/offline-mode/).

This review does not establish a separate telemetry contract for every OSV subcommand. Guided remediation and package-manager execution are outside the dependency-scan procedure reviewed here.

## Trivy standalone scanning

For the standalone [Trivy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/trivy/) CLI, the scanner runs on your host. Network needs depend on the selected scanner: vulnerability and Java databases, check bundles, image registries, optional VEX sources, and Java package lookups are distinct resources. The public scanner procedure does not require an Aqua platform account; private registries can require credentials. [Connectivity guide](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/advanced/air-gap/).

Current documentation describes usage telemetry and the `--disable-telemetry` option. That option does not disable database downloads, package lookups, or update checks. Sending reports to a platform is an additional integration, not implied by choosing local report output. [Telemetry documentation](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/advanced/telemetry/).

For restricted networks, prepare the chosen scanner's databases and checks. `--offline-scan` prevents Maven Central lookups; it does not prepare databases or control their updates. Record database and check-bundle versions separately from the executable. [Network controls](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/advanced/air-gap/#offline-mode) and [database configuration](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/configuration/db/).

This scope excludes Trivy client/server mode, cloud integrations, and third-party wrappers. Their data boundaries need separate review.

## Grype with an image or SBOM

[Grype](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/grype/) matches packages against a locally cached vulnerability database. It normally checks online for a newer database on startup. The published database is available without an Anchore account; registry access depends on where the target image is stored. [Database guide](https://oss.anchore.com/docs/guides/vulnerability/database/).

The 0.119.0 configuration reference separates application-update checking, database updates, and optional external package lookups. `external-sources.enable` is false by default; enabling it can add requests such as Maven artifact identification. No dashboard upload is part of the selected local-output procedure. The cited reference does not establish a telemetry guarantee for every wrapper or integration. [Configuration reference](https://oss.anchore.com/docs/reference/grype/configuration/).

Prepare a compatible database for disconnected use and retain its build date. Database age validation can reject stale data; changing that policy changes freshness acceptance, not the underlying advisory data. Follow the [database management commands](https://oss.anchore.com/docs/reference/grype/cli/#grype-db-import) for the installed release. Image retrieval and configured remote lookups still need their own plan.

## Record the chosen boundary

In the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/), keep the installed version, host, target revision or digest, rule/database source and snapshot, enabled network features, account/service requirements, and report destination. Prepare dependencies and artifacts before a restricted-network trial, then inspect logs and actual connection behavior in that environment.

A scan that cannot retrieve required data is failed or incomplete, not a clean result. Use [finding review](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) and [CI result handling](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) to preserve that distinction.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/execution-and-data/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/execution-and-data.json).

documents.description: Choose between source analysis, bytecode bug detection, and bounded checking for a Java project.
documents.markdown:
# Java source and bytecode analysis

Start with the artifact you can provide and the claim you want to investigate. A tool can inspect a compiled class without running the application, so bytecode input does not make an analysis dynamic.

## Compare the workflows

| Tool                                                            | Input and preparation                                                                              | Main use                                                                        | How to read the result                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/)     | Source project and an extracted analysis database; preparation depends on language and build mode. | Query code behavior and data flow for security problems.                        | A query result is evidence to review; capture and query scope matter.      |
| [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/) | Java class files or JARs, with dependency classes as needed.                                       | Detect known Java bug patterns; add Find Security Bugs for its security checks. | Record whether plugins were enabled and whether classes were missing.      |
| [JBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jbmc/)         | Java bytecode, entry point, library models, and exploration settings.                              | Check exceptions and user assertions within a modeled scope.                    | Distinguish a counterexample, bounded success, and an incomplete analysis. |

[Open the three-tool comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fcodeql%2Ctools%2Fspotbugs%2Ctools%2Fjbmc) for costs, setup, and source references.

## A small evaluation

Choose one Java revision with a reproducible build. Include a small null-access or array-access defect and its corrected version.

1. Record the JDK, dependency versions, and generated class-file version.
2. Prepare each tool's actual inputs. A shared source revision alone does not guarantee all three tools see equivalent code.
3. Record enabled rules or properties, missing classes, and analysis failures.
4. Inspect the evidence for the defect and compare the corrected revision.
5. Keep a small-case result separate from any claim about whole-project coverage.

The worked examples on the SpotBugs and JBMC pages are illustrative and have not been analyzed locally.

## Add execution tests

[Jazzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jazzer/) adds a dynamic workflow for JVM code. Compile a callable fuzz test, let the fuzzer vary its inputs, and use assertions or enabled detectors to identify failures. Its JUnit integration defaults to regression testing; enable fuzzing mode when you intend to generate new inputs.

SpotBugs inspecting class files and Jazzer executing instrumented classes both use compiled artifacts. Their conclusions differ: one reports code patterns, while the other reports failures from exercised behavior. A fuzzing run without a failure is not a proof that other inputs are safe.

## Avoid misleading comparisons

A scanner can report a pattern that a verifier never checks because its entry point cannot reach the code. A verifier can fail an assertion that no supplied scanner rule attempts to enforce. Matching the intended question is more useful than ranking raw issue counts.

Likewise, JVM bytecode is not a native executable. The Binaries filter groups compiled inputs, while each tool's notes identify the format and version requirements. The [SpotBugs documentation](https://spotbugs.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html) and [JBMC quickstart](https://www.cprover.org/jbmc/) describe their class-file workflows.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/java-analysis.json).

documents.markdown:
# Choosing memory-error checks

Memory errors can be investigated before execution or while tests exercise a program. Choose a workflow that fits the source, build control, and executable you actually have.

## Compare the workflows

| Starting point                               | Tools to consider                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Preparation                                                       | Important limit                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Source and build configuration               | [Infer Pulse](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/infer/), [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/), [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/) | Capture or configure the source analysis.                         | Models and selected checkers determine coverage.                                        |
| Source plus an instrumentable build          | [AddressSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/)                                                                                                                                            | Compile and link with instrumentation, then run tests or fuzzing. | It checks executed behavior and does not diagnose every class of memory defect.         |
| Uninitialized-value use with rebuild control | [MemorySanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/memory-sanitizer/)                                                                                                                                              | Instrument the program and arrange compatible dependencies.       | Incomplete instrumentation can produce misleading reports; platform restrictions apply. |
| Rust code and a Cargo test suite             | [Miri](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/miri/)                                                                                                                                                                     | Use a compatible nightly toolchain and interpreted tests.         | Supported operations and exercised executions limit coverage.                           |
| A compatible native executable               | [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/), [Dr. Memory](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dr-memory/)                                                                                | Run it under the selected checker with a reproducible workload.   | Platform support, workload coverage, and runtime overhead matter.                       |
| A precise property and environment model     | [CBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/), [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/), [Polyspace Code Prover](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/polyspace-code-prover/)           | Configure bounds, contracts, ranges, or other required modeling.  | Proof claims depend on the model and completeness conditions.                           |

[Compare Infer, AddressSanitizer, and Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Finfer%2Ctools%2Faddress-sanitizer%2Ctools%2Fvalgrind-memcheck).

On native Windows x64 with source and rebuild access, start with [Find a memory error on Windows](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/). It gives one MSVC AddressSanitizer setup, a faulty program, and a corrected run; its validation status is stated on that page. This is separate from the Clang/LLVM catalog entry.

If you only have an executable, consider [Dr. Memory's Windows example](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dr-memory/). It instruments execution without requiring a sanitizer build. Installation alone does not establish compatibility: check the selected release against the actual OS, architecture, and application, and keep symbols for useful diagnostic locations. [Compare Dr. Memory, Memcheck, and AddressSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fdr-memory%2Ctools%2Fvalgrind-memcheck%2Ctools%2Faddress-sanitizer) before choosing a setup.

## A useful first experiment

Use the [Windows MSVC experiment](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/) or the illustrative [Clang AddressSanitizer example](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/#first-try) as a controlled starting point. Keep two revisions: the invalid index and a corrected index.

For a static tool, verify that the intended function was included in analysis. For a runtime tool, verify that the test actually reaches the access. Record build flags and the exercised input with each report.

Then try a defect outside that first check's scope. For example, [Memcheck's manual](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/mc-manual.html) documents uninitialized-value checks, while [AddressSanitizer's documented checks](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html) focus on other memory errors. Shared Memory safety tags do not imply identical coverage.

## Add fuzzing deliberately

[AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/) and [libFuzzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/libfuzzer/) can generate executions. A sanitizer makes certain memory errors observable during those executions. The generator and the detector serve different roles.

A crash count is not a count of unique defects. Save, minimize, and reproduce inputs before drawing conclusions.

## Check undefined behavior

[UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/undefined-behavior-sanitizer/) adds selected arithmetic and pointer checks to instrumented executions, including signed integer overflow. Its check groups differ from AddressSanitizer's memory-error coverage. [Compare ASan, UBSan, and TSan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Faddress-sanitizer%2Ctools%2Fundefined-behavior-sanitizer%2Ctools%2Fthread-sanitizer) and choose the checks appropriate to the suspected defect.

## Races are another question

Two threads can access a valid allocation without appropriate synchronization. [ThreadSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/thread-sanitizer/) checks for observed data races; it complements memory-bounds checking. Use separate sanitizer builds and representative concurrent workloads.

A clean test run is evidence about the exercised behavior, not all possible paths and schedules.

[Valgrind Helgrind](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-helgrind/) offers another native concurrency workflow; [the Go race detector](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/go-race-detector/) covers race-enabled Go builds.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/memory-error-detection.json).

documents.title: Check a queue model with TLC
documents.description: Find a queue-capacity invariant violation, inspect its state trace, and repeat the same check after correcting the transition guard.
documents.markdown:
# Check a queue model with TLC

[TLC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/tlc/) explores reachable states of a TLA+ model. This example
models only a queue's occupancy. The intended property is that occupancy never
exceeds capacity. It contains no message contents, FIFO ordering, threads,
network failures, or implementation code.

The faulty and corrected modules use the same configuration and properties.
Changing only the enqueue guard makes the difference visible in a short trace.

## Prepare the example

Use [Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/) to obtain the repository, then open
`examples/tlc`. You need Python 3 to run the small download/recording scripts and
a working Java runtime for TLC. The retained run used Python 3.13.15 and an x64
Oracle JDK 25.0.4.1 on Windows 11. Other host/JVM combinations were not executed
for this example.

Download and verify the official archive pinned by `tool-lock.json`:

```sh
python fetch_tool.py
```

The script fetches `tla2tools.jar` from the official `v1.7.4` release and verifies
its byte count, the release's published SHA-1 checksum, and the recorded SHA-256.
It stores the archive in `.tools/`; it does not install Java or change your PATH.
The versioned archive reports **TLC2 Version 2.19**, so distinguish the archive's
release tag from TLC's own version string.

## Understand the property

Both modules start with `queued = 0`. An enqueue adds one and a dequeue subtracts
one when the queue is nonempty. `Queue.cfg` sets `Capacity = 2`, selects `Init`
and `Next`, and checks `TypeOK` and `WithinCapacity`.

The invariant is the same in both modules:

```text
WithinCapacity == queued <= Capacity
```

The faulty enqueue guard permits another item when occupancy already equals
capacity:

```text
Enqueue == /\ queued <= Capacity
           /\ queued' = queued + 1
```

`/\` means conjunction. The primed variable `queued'` denotes the next state's
value. In `QueueCorrected.tla`, the guard uses `<` instead of `<=`.

## Run both models

If `java` resolves to a working Java executable, run:

```sh
python run.py
```

If your launcher is missing or does not start the intended runtime, pass the
executable's full path. The recorded Windows run used:

```powershell
python run.py --java "C:/Program Files/Java/jdk-25.0.4.1/bin/java.exe"
```

Replace that path with your installed Java executable when it differs. The
runner verifies the pinned archive, copies the two model inputs into separate
run directories, and invokes the CLI with one worker, a 256 MiB Java heap,
fingerprint polynomial 0, and seed 1. It uses the default breadth-first
model-checking mode, not random simulation. It writes stdout, stderr, commands,
exit codes, runtime versions, and input hashes beneath `.runs/`.

The runner succeeds only when the faulty model reports the expected invariant
violation with a nonzero process exit and the corrected model reports completion
without an error and exits zero. It refuses to overwrite a nonempty explicit
`--output-dir`.

## Interpret the retained result

The [execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/tlc/evidence.md)
links the complete output and exact commands from November 12, 2026.

| Model            | Observed result                        | Process exit | Distinct states reported |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------ |
| `QueueFaulty`    | `WithinCapacity` violated              | 12           | 4                        |
| `QueueCorrected` | Model checking completed with no error | 0            | 3                        |

The faulty trace shows `queued` taking values 0, 1, 2, and 3. The transition out
of the full queue is the counterexample. That run stops at the reported
violation; its state count is not evidence that all later behavior was checked.

The corrected run reports five generated states, three distinct states, and
zero states remaining on the queue. It finishes the configured finite search
and finds no violation of the selected invariants. TLC uses state fingerprints;
its completion output also reports a collision-probability estimate.

## Keep the claim within the model

This result applies to capacity 2 and the stated transitions. It is not a proof
for every capacity, an unbounded queue, or a production queue implementation.
No liveness property was selected: a safety invariant does not establish that
an item is eventually removed. Larger models can fail to finish because of
state-space growth or resource limits; those are incomplete checks.

To adapt the example, first decide what states, transitions, failures, and
properties matter for your system. Record any fairness assumptions or
state-space constraints. Check that the model can reach intended states and
transitions instead of obtaining a vacuous success by excluding them. Retain
each model/configuration pair with its [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/).

For verifying contracts against implementation code, compare
[Dafny](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dafny/) and [CBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/). A design model and an
implementation need a separate argument or check connecting their behavior.

Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/model-checking/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/model-checking.json).

- **Execution scope:** TLC 2.19 from v1.7.4, Oracle Java 25.0.4.1 and Python 3.13.15 on Windows 11; capacity-2 queue occupancy and two invariants. No liveness properties or application implementation were checked.
- [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/tlc/evidence.md)

documents.description: Run Ruff and mypy against the same small project, inspect separate reports, and repeat the checks after a correction.
documents.markdown: # Check Python linting and types together [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) and [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) answer different questions. This recipe gives both the same fixture: an unused import and a call that passes text to an integer parameter. Ruff checks only `F401`; mypy checks the annotated call. Neither runs the target program. Start with [Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/) to download or clone the repository. From the downloaded repository's root, enter the fixture directory: ```powershell Set-Location examples/python-checks ``` [`examples/python-checks`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/python-checks) contains `bad/greeting.py`, the corrected `good/greeting.py`, a shared `pyproject.toml`, pinned requirements, and `run_checks.py`. **Executed on Windows with Python 3.13.15.** Both expected findings appeared in the faulty file and both checks were clean on the corrected file. The [execution record and reports](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/python-checks/evidence.md) retain the environment and tested input hashes. Other hosts have not been run for this recipe. ## Prepare an isolated environment Use Python 3.13 and the pinned Ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2 releases. These versions are a reproducible example, not a recommendation to downgrade an existing project. The target Python version is also set to 3.13 in `pyproject.toml`. On Windows, select an interpreter and check it before creating the environment: ```powershell $Python = "python" & $Python --version ``` Expect `Python 3.13.x`. If that command is missing or reports another version, set `$Python` to your Python 3.13 executable, such as `$Python = "C:\path\to\Python313\python.exe"`, and repeat the check. Continue from `examples/python-checks` once the version matches: ```powershell & $Python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` On Linux or macOS, use `.venv/bin/python` in place of the Windows interpreter path. Installing the pinned packages requires package-index access. The fixture has no application dependencies or service credentials. ## Check the faulty version Run both checks and keep their reports: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py bad --output reports/bad ``` The runner verifies versions, runs each tool separately, and saves commands, input hashes, host details, versions, and return codes in `run.json`. Diagnostics go in `ruff.json` and `mypy.txt`, with separate stderr files. Read both reports. Use a new output directory for each rerun; the runner refuses to overwrite earlier reports. It records setup failures and retains partial output on timeout. The expected signals are: | Tool | Expected finding | Meaning | | ---- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ruff | `F401` for `math` | The imported module is unused. | | mypy | `arg-type` at `greeting("three")` | The argument is text, but the parameter is annotated as an integer. | The runner returns `1` when the checks complete with findings, `0` when both complete without findings, and `2` when either cannot complete. These are this runner's gate rules, not universal analyzer exit codes. Tool completion is recorded separately from the gate in `run.json`. ## Check the correction The corrected file removes the unused import and calls `greeting(3)`. Run the same configuration against it: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py good --output reports/good ``` Both reports should be clean for this fixture. The known defects and correction show that the selected checks are active. They do not measure general defect coverage or prove that the program meets every requirement. ## Use it on your project `run_checks.py` accepts only `bad` and `good`; it is a demonstration runner. For your code, run the tools directly. From `examples/python-checks`, keep the checker interpreter's absolute path, then enter your project's root: ```powershell $CheckPython = (Resolve-Path .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe).Path Set-Location "C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT" ``` Replace `C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT` with your project directory. Use its existing analyzer configuration. If it has none, add these tables to its root `pyproject.toml`, creating the file only if absent. Merge settings into any existing tables instead of replacing the file: ```toml [tool.ruff] target-version = "py313" [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E4", "E7", "E9", "F"] [tool.mypy] python_version = "3.13" strict = true show_error_codes = true pretty = false ``` Match both target-version settings to the Python version your project supports. The fixture selects only `F401`; this starting selection adds other Pyflakes and selected pycodestyle checks. Review the [Ruff configuration](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/) for your project. If your settings live in `ruff.toml` or `mypy.ini`, use those paths in the corresponding config arguments below. The checker environment needs access to your project's dependencies and type stubs. Install the project's declared dependencies and needed stub packages in that environment, or use a project environment with the checkers installed by setting `$CheckPython` to its interpreter. Resolve [missing imports and stubs](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html#missing-imports) before treating a clean result as useful type coverage. Choose one small source directory and a new report directory for this run: ```powershell $Target = ".\src\YOUR_PACKAGE" $Reports = ".\check-reports\first-run" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Reports -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null & $CheckPython -m ruff check --no-fix --no-cache --config pyproject.toml ` --output-format json $Target > "$Reports\ruff.json" 2> "$Reports\ruff.stderr.txt" $RuffExit = $LASTEXITCODE $RuffExit | Set-Content "$Reports\ruff.exit.txt" & $CheckPython -m mypy --no-incremental --cache-dir "$Reports\mypy-cache" ` --config-file pyproject.toml $Target > "$Reports\mypy.txt" 2> "$Reports\mypy.stderr.txt" $MypyExit = $LASTEXITCODE $MypyExit | Set-Content "$Reports\mypy.exit.txt" ``` Replace `src\YOUR_PACKAGE` with the directory you want checked. Use a different `$Reports` path for every run; stop if directory creation fails. These commands make no automatic source fixes. Read `ruff.json`, `mypy.txt`, and both stderr files with their separate exit codes. Ruff returns `0` for no findings, `1` for findings, and `2` for a failed run. A completed mypy run reports either success or a diagnostic summary; an empty report or a setup error is not a clean result. Review and correct findings, then repeat with a new report directory. Record the source revision, selected configuration, exclusions, and environment using the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Keep diagnostics separate; do not compare raw issue counts as measures of quality. Use the [CI result-handling guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) to decide which completed findings block a change and how to retain failed or incomplete runs. ## Sources - [Python virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/venv.html) - [Ruff rule selection and exit behavior](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/) - [Ruff 0.14.3 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/ruff/0.14.3/) - [mypy 1.18.2 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/mypy/1.18.2/) - [mypy file and import scope](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html) Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/python-checks.json). - **Documentation reviewed:** Not recorded - **Execution evidence:** recorded - **Execution scope:** Windows with Python 3.13.15, Ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2; selected findings in faulty and corrected examples. Other hosts were not executed. - [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/python-checks/evidence.md) Documentation review is separate from execution evidence. A recorded execution applies only to its stated environment and scope; not-recorded means no structured execution record is supplied.
