documents.title: actionlint
documents.description: Check GitHub Actions workflow syntax, expressions, and action usage.
documents.markdown: # actionlint ## Where it fits actionlint can catch workflow problems before a CI run. It understands workflow keys and expression types, giving it a more specific role than a general YAML parser. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** Use the [actionlint 1.7.7 release](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/releases/tag/v1.7.7) archive matching your host OS and CPU, and record `actionlint -version`. Save this local file as `workflow.yml`; there is no need to upload it to GitHub: ```yaml name: Example on: push jobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo ready unexpected-key: true ``` Check the workflow structure with the optional script linters disabled: ```sh actionlint -shellcheck= -pyflakes= workflow.yml ``` Expect an unexpected-key diagnostic for the step. Remove `unexpected-key: true` and rerun; that diagnostic should disappear. This exercises actionlint's own workflow checks without installing ShellCheck or Pyflakes. The [check reference](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/blob/main/docs/checks.md#check-unexpected-keys) and [usage guide](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/blob/main/docs/usage.md) describe the diagnostic and integration flags. For a real repository, check its `.github/workflows` files and configure custom runner labels when needed. Enable external script linters deliberately; [ShellCheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/shellcheck/) findings still depend on the selected shell context. ## Read the diagnostic context Review the expression, input, or workflow field named by the report. Keep a real CI run as part of validation: credentials, network access, service behavior, and job runtime are outside a static workflow check. - **Summary:** Check GitHub Actions workflow syntax, expressions, and action usage. - **Use it for:** Check GitHub Actions workflow syntax, expressions, and action usage. - **What you need:** Run against a repository's workflow files or provide individual YAML paths. documents.title: AddressSanitizer (Clang)
documents.description: Detect selected memory errors while executing a program built with AddressSanitizer instrumentation.
documents.markdown: # AddressSanitizer (Clang) ## Where it fits AddressSanitizer adds a memory-error detector to executions generated by tests or fuzzers. It pairs naturally with [AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/) or [libFuzzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/libfuzzer/). For a native Windows x64 route using Visual Studio 2022, follow [Find a memory error on Windows with MSVC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/). That separate guide states its validation status and supplies setup, a faulty run, and a correction. This catalog entry and its metadata remain specific to Clang/LLVM. ## First try **Illustrative example, not run here.** With Clang and its sanitizer runtime installed on a supported host, save `bounds.c`: ```c #include int main(void) { int *values = malloc(2 * sizeof(*values)); if (!values) return 1; values[2] = 7; free(values); return 0; } ``` Build and run this small test in a Unix-style shell on a supported host: ```sh clang -O0 -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer bounds.c -o bounds ./bounds ``` For Windows PowerShell, use a compiler environment with `clang`, its C linker/libraries, and the matching AddressSanitizer runtime available. This uses the `clang` driver, not `clang-cl`; these commands are also illustrative and have not been run here: ```powershell clang -O0 -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer bounds.c -o bounds.exe .\bounds.exe ``` Before choosing this route, confirm the compiler target and runtime match your executable's architecture. A Windows label alone does not establish that your toolchain or dependencies are compatible. Representative report outline, not captured output; addresses and most stack frames are omitted: ```text ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 4 #0 main ... bounds.c:5 ... allocated ... #0 ... malloc ... #1 main ... bounds.c:3 ``` The error names the kind of invalid access. The first stack points to the write, and the allocation stack points to the two-element allocation. Index 2 is outside that allocation; valid indices are 0 and 1. Correct the index and repeat. The report format and symbol locations depend on the platform and available debug information. For toolchain installation and platform-specific setup, use the [Clang AddressSanitizer guide](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html). ## Interpret coverage A successful execution only covers the behavior that ran. Keep the build flags, workload, and suppression settings with the report. See [memory-error detection](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/) to compare an instrumented build with static checking and Memcheck's executable instrumentation. If you only have an existing executable, check [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) or [Dr. Memory](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dr-memory/) for a compatible host and binary. They use different runtime checking workflows; check the platform limits before choosing one. - **Summary:** Detect selected memory errors while executing a program built with AddressSanitizer instrumentation. - **Use it for:** Use AddressSanitizer when you can rebuild C or C++ code and want to catch memory errors while running tests or fuzzing. - **What you need:** C or C++ source, a supported Clang toolchain, and permission to rebuild and run tests. Compile and link with AddressSanitizer instrumentation; an existing executable alone is not enough. - **What you get:** A runtime report identifying a detected memory error, with stack and allocation information when available. - **Checks and limits:** It checks instrumented code that actually runs. A clean run says nothing about unexecuted paths, and not every kind of memory error is covered. - **Finding scope:** Detects instrumented, executed memory errors such as out-of-bounds access and use-after-free. It does not cover all undefined behavior or general uninitialized-value use. ## Compatibility and scope - **Also known as:** ASan, Address Sanitizer - **Analysis mode:** Dynamic - **What it examines:** Binaries - **Context:** Native programs, Libraries - **Techniques:** Runtime memory checking, Sanitizer instrumentation - **Finding categories:** Memory safety - **Where it runs:** Supported Clang/runtime OS and CPU combinations. The documentation lists Linux, macOS, Windows, and other platforms with differences in available checks; verify the chosen target. - **Languages / ecosystem:** C, C++ - **Language support:** This entry covers Clang/LLVM C/C++ workflows. Other compiler integrations and language frontends have their own support limits. - **Edition and scope:** Clang/LLVM AddressSanitizer. Leak and stack-lifetime checks have platform and configuration limits. ## Cost and editions - **Cost:** Free - **Cost conditions:** Free compiler/runtime component. No paid analysis edition is required; instrumented execution uses additional memory and compute. - **License category:** Open source - **License:** Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception for current LLVM compiler-rt; some components retain other notices Cost information checked 2026-09-22. Runtimes, hosting, and compute may cost extra. Free trials are not counted as free editions. ## Sources and evidence [Official website](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html) - [Current checks, usage, and platform limits](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html) - [Project guide to C/C++ instrumentation](https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizer) - [Runtime licensing](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/compiler-rt/LICENSE.TXT) Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/). [JSON record and content revision](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/tools/address-sanitizer.json). - **Documentation reviewed:** 2026-09-22 - **Execution evidence:** recorded - **Execution scope:** The Windows example ran MSVC AddressSanitizer with compiler 19.44.35229 on native Windows Server 2022 x64 in CI. The faulty C fixture reported a four-byte heap-buffer-overflow write at bounds.c:5 and exited 1; the correction exited 0 with no output. This is evidence for the MSVC Windows route, not a Clang execution, fresh toolchain installation, ARM64 support, or unexecuted paths. - [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/agent-knowledge/ci/42653327079/run.json) - [Execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/agent-knowledge/ci/42653327079/source.json) Documentation review is separate from execution evidence. documents.title: AFL++
documents.description: Mutate inputs using execution feedback to find crashes, hangs, and failures exposed by a fuzzing target.
documents.markdown:
# AFL++

## What it does

AFL++ evolves a collection of input samples using feedback from repeated target executions. Inputs that expose new behavior help guide later mutations. It saves interesting failures so you can reproduce and investigate them.

The target may read input from a file or standard input, or use a custom harness for a library. A small deterministic target generally makes failures easier to reproduce.

## Source available versus binary only

With source, compile the target with compatible instrumentation. Without source, a supported mode can obtain feedback through mechanisms such as emulation or dynamic instrumentation. Those modes have distinct platform and architecture restrictions.

Both workflows execute a binary. This is dynamic testing, even though a source build or binary preparation step happens first.

## What counts as a failure?

Crashes and timeouts are useful starting points. A sanitizer can make otherwise silent memory errors visible; an assertion can expose a violated invariant. Without an appropriate failure detector, an incorrect output may look like an ordinary successful execution.

Deduplicate and replay failures before estimating their significance. More coverage or more saved crashes does not directly measure the number of distinct vulnerabilities.

See [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) for the comparison with property-based testing and temporal falsification.

- **Summary:** Mutate inputs using execution feedback to find crashes, hangs, and failures exposed by a fuzzing target.
- **Use it for:** Mutate inputs using execution feedback to find crashes, hangs, and failures exposed by a fuzzing target.
- **What you need:** Build an instrumented target when source is available, or configure a supported binary-only mode. Provide an input interface or harness, seed inputs, and a reproducible execution environment.
- **Checks and limits:** Crash and hang detection is built in. Memory diagnostics depend on instrumentation such as sanitizers; specification failures require an assertion or another failure signal in the target.
- **Finding scope:** Crash and hang detection is built in. Memory diagnostics depend on instrumentation such as sanitizers; specification failures require an assertion or another failure signal in the target.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Also known as:** AFL plus plus, AFLplusplus
- **Analysis mode:** Dynamic
- **What it examines:** Binaries
- **Context:** Native programs, Libraries, Native binaries
- **Techniques:** Coverage-guided fuzzing
- **Finding categories:** Crashes and hangs, Memory safety, Specification violations
- **Where it runs:** Linux is a primary workflow. macOS is documented with mode restrictions; binary-only modes depend on architecture, OS, and emulator support. Use a compatible Linux environment from Windows.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** C, C++, Language independent
- **Language support:** C/C++ source builds are documented workflows. Binary-only modes work at the executable level, so support depends on architecture and execution mode rather than a universal source-language list.
- **Edition and scope:** Current stable repository documentation identifying version 5.03c. Earlier releases can have different licensing; the current license is not inferred from older Apache-only descriptions.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free

documents.description: Explore compiled programs with a programmable binary-analysis and symbolic-execution framework.
documents.markdown:
# angr

## When to use it

Choose angr when the question is about behavior inside a compiled artifact and you can write the analysis needed to answer it. For a predefined set of binary weakness checks, compare [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/).

## Worked example: find an input for a branch

**Illustrative example, not run here.** On a compatible native build host, save `branch_check.c`:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    puts(getchar() == 'K' ? "accepted" : "rejected");
    return 0;
}
```

Compile it with `cc -O0 branch_check.c -o branch_check`. In a Python environment with angr installed, run:

```python
import angr
import claripy

project = angr.Project("./branch_check", auto_load_libs=False)
symbol = claripy.BVS("input_byte", 8)
stream = angr.SimFileStream(name="stdin", content=symbol, has_end=True)
state = project.factory.full_init_state(args=["./branch_check"], stdin=stream)
paths = project.factory.simulation_manager(state)
paths.explore(find=lambda candidate: b"accepted" in candidate.posix.dumps(1))

if paths.found:
    print(paths.found[0].posix.dumps(0))
else:
    print("No matching state found in this exploration")
```

The intended witness is the byte `K`. This is a reachability exercise; the branch is not itself a security defect.

## Limits

Models of library calls, startup state, memory, and system behavior affect the result. Many branches can make exploration expensive. Finding no state does not establish impossibility unless the exploration and model justify that conclusion.

Reproduce a witness against the original program before drawing conclusions about concrete behavior.

See [static method results](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/) to distinguish symbolic path constraints from concrete execution.

- **Summary:** Explore compiled programs with a programmable binary-analysis and symbolic-execution framework.
- **Use it for:** Explore compiled programs with a programmable binary-analysis and symbolic-execution framework.
- **What you need:** Load a supported binary and configure an entry state, symbolic inputs, environment models, and search goals. Bare-metal targets need additional loader and memory configuration.
- **Checks and limits:** You must encode the behavior or failure condition to investigate. Finding a reachable state is not automatically a vulnerability; angr is a framework, not a fixed vulnerability-rule scanner.
- **Finding scope:** You must encode the behavior or failure condition to investigate. Finding a reachable state is not automatically a vulnerability; angr is a framework, not a fixed vulnerability-rule scanner.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Binaries
- **Context:** Native binaries, Firmware
- **Techniques:** Binary analysis, Symbolic execution
- **Finding categories:** Specification violations
- **Where it runs:** Python with compatible native dependencies, or the project container. Check wheel availability for the host; a source build can require C/C++ and Rust toolchains.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Language independent
- **Language support:** Targets are supported executable formats and architectures. Python is the scripting interface, not a claim that this entry analyzes Python source.
- **Edition and scope:** Offline binary loading and symbolic execution. Concrete-execution integrations and separate analysis packages are outside this entry's mode tags.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free framework and Python API. No paid tier is required for the documented symbolic-execution workflow.

## Where it fits

## Design a narrow harness

Start with one parser or library operation. Handle expected input rejection deliberately while allowing unexpected failures to remain visible. For a native extension, follow the separate build guide before interpreting coverage or sanitizer findings.

documents.title: axe-core
documents.description: Evaluate a rendered web page against automated accessibility rules and report affected elements.
documents.markdown:
# axe-core

## First try

Use the [worked browser example](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/browser-testing/) to compare a
page whose search input has no accessible name with a corrected page containing
an explicit label. The fixture pins axe-core through its dependency lockfile and
scans the initial page with `wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, and `wcag21aa` tags.

After the example setup, run from its directory:

```sh
pnpm test:bad
pnpm test:good
```

**Executed on the recorded Windows host.** The faulty scan reported rule `label`
against `#tool-query`; the corrected scan reported no violations. Neither scan
had incomplete results. The
[execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/browser-testing/record.json)
retains engine/browser versions, viewport, rule-result IDs, and input hashes.

## Interpret the result categories

Inspect each violation's rule ID, affected nodes, help URL, and failure summary.
Fix the cause and repeat the same scan so a changed rule set or omitted element
does not explain the disappearance. Keep `incomplete` results visible for human
review. Passed rules describe evaluated conditions; inapplicable rules did not
find relevant content in that scan.

The absence of violations is scoped to the selected rules and page state.
Open dialogs, expand menus, exercise validation errors, and scan other relevant
states explicitly. Add keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, and usability assessment
appropriate to the application. Automated testing alone cannot establish full
accessibility or conformance.

## Keep accessibility and behavior checks separate

The example's capability-search bug can exist even when the input has a correct
label. Its missing label can exist even when search results are functionally
correct. [Playwright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/playwright/) assertions check the selected workflow;
axe-core checks the selected accessibility rules. Neither result substitutes
for the other.

- **Summary:** Evaluate a rendered web page against automated accessibility rules and report affected elements.
- **Use it for:** Find automatically detectable accessibility issues in a specific rendered web-page state.
- **What you need:** Install the project's locked axe integration, render a test page, select its intended state and rule tags, run a scan, and retain the full results before asserting on violations.
- **What you get:** Violations with rule IDs, affected nodes and guidance, plus passed, inapplicable and incomplete rule results.
- **Checks and limits:** Automated rules detect only part of accessibility. A scan with no violations does not establish WCAG conformance, usable keyboard behavior, or successful assistive-technology use.
- **Finding scope:** Violations apply to the rule set, page content, and state actually scanned. Incomplete results need review; unvisited states and checks that require people are outside the result.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Also known as:** axe, axe core
- **Analysis mode:** Dynamic
- **What it examines:** Running applications
- **Context:** Web applications, Rendered web pages, Browser user interfaces
- **Techniques:** Automated accessibility testing
- **Finding categories:** Accessibility issues
- **Where it runs:** A supported browser and JavaScript test harness. This route uses @axe-core/playwright with Playwright's browser installation; the adapter's supported Node.js version can be stricter than the core engine's.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** HTML
- **Language support:** Rules inspect the rendered HTML page and browser state. The backend implementation language is not restricted to HTML, and this profile does not describe static HTML source linting.
- **Edition and scope:** axe-core 4.14.0 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0. The executed example covers selected WCAG-tagged rules on one initial page; it is not a conformance audit or a review of commercial axe products.

- **Cost conditions:** The open-source engine and Playwright integration require no hosted account. Commercial Deque products, manual assessment, and execution infrastructure are separate.

documents.markdown:
# Bandit

## What it does

Bandit parses Python files and runs security checks against their abstract syntax trees. Its plugins look for patterns associated with unsafe behavior and produce findings for review.

## When it is useful

Use it as a focused security check in a Python development workflow.

## What to keep in mind

A flagged pattern needs context: an API call may be intentional, or its input may already be constrained. Bandit is not a proof that a project is secure, and its checks do not replace runtime testing or a review of application logic.

## Getting started

The official documentation links installation, configuration, plugin, and CI/CD guides. Begin with the default checks on a small Python project, then review findings before adding exclusions.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used Bandit for its Python implementation. Its results illustrate how a focused analyzer can produce a different report from a multi-language platform. They do not establish that every reported pattern is a confirmed vulnerability.

See [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for interpreting counts and [SAST adoption](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-adoption/) for planning the effort needed to review them.

- **Summary:** Find common security issues in Python source code using checks against its syntax tree.
- **Use it for:** Find common security issues in Python source code using checks against its syntax tree.
- **What you need:** No application build or runtime harness. Supply Python source and configure plugins, exclusions, and severity thresholds.
- **Checks and limits:** Selected security-pattern plugins; a flagged call requires context and is not a demonstrated exploit.

documents.markdown:
# Binwalk

## What it does

Binwalk helps identify what a firmware image or other binary container may contain. A result gives an offset and a candidate format, which can guide extraction and inspection of an embedded filesystem, archive, or executable.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** In a supported Binwalk 3 environment, scan a firmware image you already have:

```sh
binwalk firmware.bin
```

Review the reported offsets and formats. Enable extraction separately if needed, using the release's documented options and extractor dependencies. The command above is the initial identification step.

## Limits

A recognizable header is evidence of a candidate format, not a guarantee that extraction will succeed. Compression and encryption can both affect entropy, so an entropy result needs context.

Binwalk does not by itself determine whether an embedded component has a known CVE. After locating an artifact, use [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) for supported component/advisory matching or [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) to inspect recovered code. Keep the original image and offsets so findings can be traced back to their source.

- **Summary:** Identify embedded file formats and inspect firmware images and other binary containers.
- **Use it for:** Identify embedded file formats and inspect firmware images and other binary containers.
- **What you need:** Supply a firmware image or other file. Extraction can require external utilities; the documented Docker build supplies a fuller dependency environment.
- **Checks and limits:** Reports candidate embedded formats and offsets. Entropy can suggest compressed or encrypted regions, but neither signatures nor entropy establish a vulnerability.
- **Finding scope:** Reports candidate embedded formats and offsets. Entropy can suggest compressed or encrypted regions, but neither signatures nor entropy establish a vulnerability.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Binaries
- **Context:** Firmware, Embedded files, Archives
- **Techniques:** Binary analysis, Signature matching, Entropy analysis
- **Finding categories:** Embedded file formats
- **Where it runs:** The project primarily supports 64-bit Linux and documents an Ubuntu-based Docker setup. Windows and macOS are largely untested according to its platform guide.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Language independent
- **Language support:** Operates on file bytes and embedded formats. Rust is the implementation language of version 3, not a source language analyzed by this workflow.
- **Edition and scope:** Binwalk version 3. Earlier version 2 tutorials can have different dependencies, commands, and licensing.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free version 3 scanner and extraction framework. This entry does not cover separate commercial firmware-analysis services or older version 2 licensing.

documents.description: Generate malformed protocol messages and exercise a running service through a configurable test session.
documents.markdown:
# boofuzz

## What it does

boofuzz separates the protocol description from the target connection and failure monitoring. A request graph can establish a session before mutating a later message. Supported connections include TCP, UDP, and serial interfaces.

## First try

Use the [supplied PING target and harness](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/protocol-ping) for a complete local response check. It includes a loopback server, faulty and corrected modes, two selected mutations, response validation, readiness/reset handling, and stop instructions.

**Executed on 2026-11-06:** boofuzz 0.4.2 on Windows/Python 3.12.16. The faulty target omitted its reply to a valid `PING TRIGGER` request. The response callback reported that violation; the corrected target passed both selected cases. This was a finite protocol demonstration, not a process-crash test or a broad fuzzing campaign.

Each run retains requests, replies, configuration hashes, console output, and a boofuzz database. The [execution observations](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/audits/remaining-work/executions/boofuzz) preserve the results separately from expected behavior. Adapt the message model, monitor, and reset procedure to the real target before expanding the mutation set.

## Limits

A lost connection may be expected rejection or a real failure; inspect the service and reproduce the input. Protocol state, checksums, authentication, and target recovery can require custom harness work.

Compare [Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/) or [RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) when an HTTP API definition can drive test generation. Compare [AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/) when an instrumentable binary and execution-feedback workflow fit better.

- **Summary:** Generate malformed protocol messages and exercise a running service through a configurable test session.
- **Use it for:** Generate malformed protocol messages and exercise a running service through a configurable test session.
- **What you need:** Describe message fields and request order, configure a target connection, and arrange monitoring and target reset. Application source is not required for network testing.
- **Checks and limits:** Failure detection depends on monitors, response checks, and callbacks you configure. Sending malformed messages alone does not identify every crash, memory error, or protocol violation.
- **Finding scope:** Failure detection depends on monitors, response checks, and callbacks you configure. Sending malformed messages alone does not identify every crash, memory error, or protocol violation.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Dynamic
- **What it examines:** Running applications
- **Context:** Network services, Protocol implementations, Embedded systems
- **Techniques:** Protocol fuzzing, Mutation-based fuzzing
- **Finding categories:** Crashes and hangs, Specification violations
- **Where it runs:** Python on a compatible host; Windows and Unix installation routes are documented. Process monitors, raw sockets, and serial connections impose additional platform requirements.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Language independent
- **Language support:** Targets services through their protocol interfaces. Python is used to describe the harness, not the language the service must be written in.
- **Edition and scope:** Stable 0.4.2 documentation for protocol definitions, sessions, and target connections. This entry does not imply built-in code-coverage feedback.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost conditions:** Free protocol-fuzzing framework. Target devices, monitoring infrastructure, and test environments are separate resources.

documents.markdown:
# Brakeman

## When to use it

Choose Brakeman when you have a Rails codebase and want checks that understand Rails conventions. General Ruby syntax support in another analyzer does not establish equivalent knowledge of Rails data flow.

## Worked example: review a Rails project

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** Install the current compatible gem, then run from the root of a Rails project you can review:

```sh
gem install brakeman
brakeman -o brakeman-report.html
```

Open the report and inspect the warning's location, confidence, and evidence. For a concrete exercise, review a controller that incorporates request data into a SQL string. Compare it with the corresponding parameterized query and re-run the scanner. Exact warnings depend on Rails version and the surrounding code.

## Free use and commercial use

The license explicitly treats scanning the licensee's own software as a permitted free use. Its defined commercial uses include offering a scanning service and distributing the scanner in a commercial product. Read the linked terms for your workflow.

Source availability does not make this an unrestricted open-source license. The catalog therefore uses Source available and Free with limits.

## What a result means

A source warning is a review lead. It does not show that authentication, routing, or deployed configuration makes the path reachable. Conversely, an unrecognized pattern can escape a check.

Combine source review with [ZAP](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/zap/) or another suitable runtime test when you need evidence about a running Rails application.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) lists Brakeman as its Ruby analyzer. That historical selection does not broaden Brakeman's documented Rails scope to arbitrary Ruby applications.

Read [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for the study's limitations. For a new evaluation, verify that the application's framework matches the tool before interpreting its report.

- **Summary:** Check Ruby on Rails source for security weaknesses using Rails-specific analysis.
- **Use it for:** Check Ruby on Rails source for security weaknesses using Rails-specific analysis.
- **What you need:** Provide the Rails application source and choose the project directory. A running Rails server, test harness, or deployed URL is not required.
- **Checks and limits:** Warnings depend on recognized Rails behavior and enabled checks. Confidence levels guide review; a warning does not establish that a deployed endpoint is exploitable.
- **Finding scope:** Warnings depend on recognized Rails behavior and enabled checks. Confidence levels guide review; a warning does not establish that a deployed endpoint is exploitable.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Source code

- **Finding categories:** Injection risks, Unsafe API use, Security misconfiguration

- **Languages / ecosystem:** Ruby

- **Edition and scope:** Current Brakeman Rails scanner and Public Use License. The repository's older MIT file does not describe the entire current distribution.

## Cost and editions

documents.markdown:
# Breach

## What it does

Breach can check recorded signals against Signal Temporal Logic (STL) requirements or repeatedly simulate a model to search for a violation. It provides Simulink integration, parameter exploration, input signal generation, and an interface for other simulators.

## When it is useful

Use it when a requirement concerns behavior over time: for example, whether a controller keeps a signal below a limit throughout a run.

## What you provide

- A simulator interface or recorded traces with named signals.
- An STL requirement and a simulation horizon.
- For falsification, allowed input or parameter ranges and a search budget.

## What to keep in mind

A monitor checks supplied traces; a falsification search generates candidates to find a violating trace. An unsuccessful search does not prove the requirement holds for all inputs. See [model and temporal falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/).

## Getting started

Follow the official README's setup and built-in demos, then work through its falsification example. Check the licenses of bundled components as well as the core license if redistributing the toolbox.

- **Summary:** Search simulations for violations of Signal Temporal Logic requirements and monitor recorded traces.
- **Use it for:** Search simulations for violations of Signal Temporal Logic requirements and monitor recorded traces.
- **What you need:** A simulator interface, signal definitions, temporal requirements, and input bounds are needed for falsification. Trace-only monitoring can use recorded data.

documents.markdown:
# capa

## Inputs

For static analysis, capa extracts features from supported artifacts such as PE, ELF, .NET modules, or shellcode. For dynamic analysis, it reads recorded behavior from a supported sandbox report. These workflows do not necessarily expose the same evidence.

The Dynamic tag describes analysis of previously observed execution. Passing a binary to the ordinary static workflow does not run it in a sandbox.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With the standalone release and its bundled resources, inspect a known test executable:

```sh
capa -vv sample.exe
```

Review each matched rule and its evidence locations. Follow interesting locations in [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) before drawing conclusions about the surrounding behavior.

## Limits

Packing can expose mostly the unpacker rather than the payload. An installer can expose its installation framework rather than the installed program. Missing features, unsupported code, and incomplete sandbox coverage all limit matching.

A capability such as file access can be ordinary application behavior. Record the rule set and analysis mode alongside the result.

## Related research

We discuss capa in our [malware sophistication paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf) as part of the binary-analysis context. We did not evaluate its accuracy or validate a capability count as a sophistication measure. See [Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/) for those limits.

- **Summary:** Match binary features or recorded execution behavior to rules describing program capabilities.
- **Use it for:** Match binary features or recorded execution behavior to rules describing program capabilities.
- **What you need:** Supply a supported binary or an existing supported sandbox report. Use the bundled rules in a standalone release, or configure rules and signatures separately for a library installation.
- **Checks and limits:** Matches capability rules to extracted evidence. A match does not establish malicious intent, a vulnerability, or that every identified static capability executed.
- **Finding scope:** Matches capability rules to extracted evidence. A match does not establish malicious intent, a vulnerability, or that every identified static capability executed.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static, Dynamic
- **What it examines:** Binaries, Execution traces
- **Context:** Native binaries, .NET assemblies, Sandbox reports
- **Techniques:** Binary analysis, Rule-based matching, Trace analysis
- **Finding categories:** Program capabilities
- **Where it runs:** Standalone distributions and documented installation routes for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Optional analysis backends have additional requirements.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Language independent
- **Language support:** Coverage depends on the binary format, architecture, analysis backend, or sandbox report format. Python is an implementation interface, not the target-language scope.
- **Edition and scope:** Static feature matching and dynamic analysis of supported CAPE, DRAKVUF, or VMRay reports. capa does not itself supply a full malware-execution sandbox.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free analyzer with a public rule collection. Producing a sandbox report or using an optional external analysis backend can involve separate tools or services.
- **License category:** Open source
- **License:** Apache-2.0

documents.title: cargo-audit
documents.description: Check Rust dependency versions against RustSec security advisories.
documents.markdown:
# cargo-audit

## Inputs

The project workflow reads `Cargo.lock` to identify resolved dependencies and consults the RustSec advisory database. It does not execute the application or require a source-analysis build.

The binary workflow can use dependency information embedded by `cargo auditable`. Without that metadata, recovery from panic strings is partial and can miss Rust crates and embedded C components. The Binaries tag therefore does not promise a complete inventory of every Rust executable.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With Cargo installed:

```sh
cargo install cargo-audit --locked
```

From a project containing `Cargo.lock`, run:

```sh
cargo audit
```

For a supported release's binary workflow:

```sh
cargo audit bin path/to/program
```

Review each identified version and advisory. Preserve the lockfile or binary revision and advisory-data date with the report.

## Limits

An inventory/advisory match is not a source defect diagnosis. For Rust source checks, compare [Clippy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clippy/) or [Kani](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/kani/). For multiple dependency ecosystems, compare [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/).

## Related research

We used Cargo-audit for Rust in our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf). Its dependency-advisory results differ in scope from source-analyzer results; see [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/).

- **Summary:** Check Rust dependency versions against RustSec security advisories.
- **Use it for:** Check Rust dependency versions against RustSec security advisories.
- **What you need:** Provide Cargo.lock and advisory data for the project workflow. Binary auditing uses embedded dependency metadata when present, or a less complete recovery method otherwise.
- **Checks and limits:** Matches identified crate versions to advisories. A match does not establish reachability or exploitability; incomplete binary inventories can miss dependencies.
- **Finding scope:** Matches identified crate versions to advisories. A match does not establish reachability or exploitability; incomplete binary inventories can miss dependencies.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Dependency metadata, Binaries
- **Context:** Cargo projects, Rust binaries
- **Techniques:** Software composition analysis, Known vulnerability detection
- **Finding categories:** Known vulnerable dependencies
- **Where it runs:** A host compatible with the selected cargo-audit release and Rust/Cargo toolchain, or a documented package-manager installation.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Rust
- **Language support:** Rust describes the dependency ecosystem. This tool does not inspect Rust source logic for new defects.
- **Edition and scope:** Current documented cargo audit and cargo audit bin workflows. Optional automatic dependency fixes and separate reachability tools are outside this entry.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free CLI and public RustSec advisory data. No paid tier is required for the documented audit workflows.

documents.title: CBMC
documents.description: Check C and C++ assertions and memory safety by translating bounded program executions into solver queries.
documents.markdown: # CBMC ## What it does CBMC converts a representation of possible C/C++ executions into constraints for a solver. It checks selected safety properties and assertions and can return a counterexample showing inputs and steps that violate a property. This can reveal defects beyond the concrete inputs in an ordinary test suite. Useful targets include small routines with strict memory-safety requirements or explicit input/output contracts. ## Bounds and proof claims Loops are unwound to explore iterations. If a chosen bound cuts off possible behavior, checking within that bound does not establish correctness beyond it. Unwinding assertions help determine whether further iterations remain possible. The harness also matters. Assumptions restrict inputs, and models of external functions determine which effects the verifier considers. An overly restrictive assumption can exclude the very behavior you intended to check. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** Install a CBMC 6.x build for your host using the [official setup guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/installation.html). Save this as `bounded.c`: ```c #include int nondet_int(void); int clamp(int value) { return value; } void harness(void) { int value = nondet_int(); __CPROVER_assume(value >= 0 && value <= 10); assert(clamp(value) <= 9); } ``` Use `harness` as the entry point and request a counterexample: ```sh cbmc bounded.c --function harness --trace ``` CBMC treats the undefined `nondet_int` return as nondeterministic. The assumption restricts it to 0 through 10. Expect the assertion to fail with `value = 10`. Change the function to `return value > 9 ? 9 : value;` and rerun. That assertion should pass under the stated assumption. This fixture has no loops, recursion, or external side effects, so it needs no loop bound. When adapting it to looping code, supply suitable unwinding bounds and inspect unwinding assertions as well as the property. Do not suppress an incomplete unwind and call the result an unbounded proof. Keep the harness, assumptions, checked properties, and bounds with the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). The [harness guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/proof-harnesses.html) and [property-checking guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/checking-properties.html) explain how these choices define the verification task. See [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) for the difference between bounded checking, fuzzing, and falsification. - **Summary:** Check C and C++ assertions and memory safety by translating bounded program executions into solver queries. - **Use it for:** Check C and C++ assertions and memory safety by translating bounded program executions into solver queries. - **What you need:** Supply source, an entry point or verification harness, assumptions, and assertions. Configure loop unwinding and model external functions; compiling and running the target as an ordinary application is not required. - **Checks and limits:** Built-in safety checks and user assertions are evaluated within the modeled environment and exploration bounds. A successful bounded check is not automatically an unbounded proof. - **Finding scope:** Built-in safety checks and user assertions are evaluated within the modeled environment and exploration bounds. A successful bounded check is not automatically an unbounded proof. ## Compatibility and scope - **Analysis mode:** Static - **What it examines:** Source code - **Context:** Source code - **Techniques:** Bounded model checking, Formal verification - **Finding categories:** Memory safety, Specification violations - **Where it runs:** Windows, Linux, and macOS; compiler and release-package prerequisites differ by host. - **Languages / ecosystem:** C, C++ - **Language support:** This entry covers CBMC for C/C++. JBMC for Java and Kani for Rust are separate tools, not additional CBMC language tags. - **Edition and scope:** CBMC 6.x C/C++ bounded checking; guarantees depend on the harness, program model, checked properties, and completeness of exploration. ## Cost and editions - **Cost:** Free - **Cost conditions:** Free open-source verifier. Optional external solvers and compute have their own requirements; no paid CBMC edition is needed for the workflow described here. - **License category:** Open source - **License:** BSD-4-Clause; bundled and optional solvers have separate licenses Cost information checked 2026-09-22. Runtimes, hosting, and compute may cost extra. Free trials are not counted as free editions. ## Sources and evidence [Official website](https://www.cprover.org/cbmc/) - [CBMC capabilities and supported hosts](https://www.cprover.org/cbmc/) - [Loop unwinding and unwinding assertions](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/faq/loop-unwinding.html) - [CBMC license](https://github.com/diffblue/cbmc/blob/develop/LICENSE) - [Installation and host setup](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/installation.html) - [Verification harnesses and assumptions](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/proof-harnesses.html) - [Property checking](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/checking-properties.html) Source: [ToolWiki page](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/). Start with one infrastructure directory and an explicit framework selection. Confirm that external modules and variable values are available before treating the scan as representative of the intended deployment.

Review the check identifier, affected resource, and relevant policy. Keep baseline exceptions and skipped rules visible in review. A passing result reflects the selected policies and available configuration; it is not a live audit of the deployed environment.

# Clang Static Analyzer

## What it does

Clang Static Analyzer performs path-sensitive analysis to find bugs in C-family programs. It reasons about possible execution paths without running the target program on concrete test inputs.

## When it is useful

Consider it when working on native code and investigating defects such as invalid pointer use. It is part of Clang and can fit into a build-oriented workflow.

## What to keep in mind

The analyzer needs an accurate view of the code and build configuration. Its modeled paths do not cover all possible program behavior. Review the available checkers and their maturity before treating their output as equally reliable.

## Getting started

Follow the analyzer's documentation for a build-integrated run. Keep the compiler configuration and enabled checker set with your results so later runs are comparable.

See [clang-tidy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-tidy/) for a configurable linting and modernization workflow that can also select Clang Static Analyzer checks. [Compare the two tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fclang-static-analyzer%2Ctools%2Fclang-tidy) before choosing the checks to run.

- **Summary:** Explore possible execution paths to find bugs in C, C++, and Objective-C code.
- **Use it for:** Explore possible execution paths to find bugs in C, C++, and Objective-C code.
- **What you need:** Supply source and accurate compiler options, commonly through a build capture or compilation database. No runtime harness.
- **Checks and limits:** Selected path-sensitive checkers, including pointer and lifetime defects. Checker maturity and modeling limit coverage.
- **Finding scope:** Selected path-sensitive checkers, including pointer and lifetime defects. Checker maturity and modeling limit coverage.

# clang-tidy

## Where it fits

Use clang-tidy for repeatable source checks during development or code review. Select the check families your project needs, and record the configuration in `.clang-tidy`.

It can invoke checks from [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/), alongside its own rules. Treat the selected checks as the scope of a run; the tool name alone does not identify that scope.

## Worked example: a null pointer constant

**Illustrative example, not run here.** With clang-tidy installed, save this C++ source as `sample.cpp`:

```cpp
int* missing_value() {
    return 0;
}
```

Select one check and supply the language standard:

```sh
clang-tidy sample.cpp '-checks=-*,modernize-use-nullptr' -- -std=c++11
```

The intended suggestion is to use `nullptr` for the returned null pointer. This command reports diagnostics without requesting automatic edits. Change `0` to `nullptr` and run it again.

## Project setup and limits

For a project, point `-p` at the directory containing its compilation database. Missing include paths, generated headers, or build definitions can prevent useful analysis.

Review fixes and run project tests before accepting them. Compare [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/) for another native-source workflow, or [compare the three tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fclang-tidy%2Ctools%2Fclang-static-analyzer%2Ctools%2Fcppcheck).

documents.description: Use Rust compiler-integrated lints to catch common mistakes and improve Rust code.
documents.markdown:
# Clippy

## What it does

Clippy adds lint diagnostics to Rust's compiler-based workflow. It identifies correctness mistakes, suspicious code, unnecessary complexity, and opportunities for more idiomatic or efficient code.

Its checks complement Rust's compiler errors. Passing the compiler and Clippy does not prove that application logic, unsafe code, or external interfaces behave correctly.

## Which lints run?

| Group          | How to interpret it                                                                |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Default groups | Include correctness, suspicious code, style, complexity, and performance patterns. |
| Pedantic       | Stricter checks that can be useful but may need exceptions.                        |
| Restriction    | Individual restrictions on otherwise valid code; choose rules deliberately.        |
| Nursery        | New lints still being developed.                                                   |

The project explicitly advises against enabling the whole restriction group: rules can be inappropriate for your project or conflict with one another. Choose checks based on your requirements.

## Inputs and workflow

Use Clippy with a compatible Rust toolchain and the project's Cargo workspace. The usual entry point is `cargo clippy`; workspace and package selection control the scope. Compiler-driven setup may execute build scripts or procedural macros even though the target application's runtime behavior is not being tested.

Different feature combinations or compilation targets may include different code. Keep those choices and the minimum supported Rust version with your lint configuration.

## A useful first evaluation

Start with the default lints on a representative package. Review diagnostic explanations before enabling stricter groups, then decide which warnings should fail CI. Promoting all warnings to errors also includes ordinary compiler warnings, so toolchain upgrades can affect that policy.

Some suggestions can be applied automatically. Review the resulting changes and run the project's tests rather than treating a suggested rewrite as proof that behavior is preserved.

- **Summary:** Use Rust compiler-integrated lints to catch common mistakes and improve Rust code.
- **Use it for:** Use Rust compiler-integrated lints to catch common mistakes and improve Rust code.
- **What you need:** A Rust/Cargo project with dependencies and chosen features. Compiler checks may run build scripts and procedural macros; no runtime test harness.

documents.description: Query a structured model of code to investigate vulnerabilities and trace data flow.
documents.markdown: # CodeQL ## First try **Documentation reviewed on November 6, 2026; not executed here.** This builder workflow covers only Python SQL injection. Other catalog capabilities were not re-reviewed. Use the [CodeQL 2.27.4 bundle](https://github.com/github/codeql-action/releases/tag/codeql-bundle-v2.27.4) for Linux x86-64 on Ubuntu 22.04. The reviewed query pack is `codeql/python-queries@1.9.0`, with `py/sql-injection` at `Security/CWE-089/SqlInjection.ql`. The tagged query/library revision is `1be292a1e54696ca543b4ad0f9b4537b9687caa7`. 1. Check that your project is eligible under the [CLI terms](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries/blob/main/LICENSE.md). The query repository's MIT license does not replace those terms. Public-repository and private-organization entitlements differ. 2. Follow the [CLI setup guide](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/find-and-fix-code-vulnerabilities/scan-from-the-command-line/set-up-codeql-cli). Make Python 3.12 available as `python3` and prepare the source and its dependencies. Use `codeql resolve packs` to confirm the query-pack version. 3. Choose a small Python project using modeled request sources and SQL APIs. The [upstream example](https://codeql.github.com/codeql-query-help/python/py-sql-injection/) shows Django request data reaching cursor queries. Check your framework/version and call shapes against the models; the example's legacy Django routing syntax is not a current application setup recipe. 4. Create a database without a build command, then analyze only the pinned query. In this example, `src` is your source directory and `codeql-python-db` must not already exist: ```sh codeql database create codeql-python-db --language=python --source-root=src codeql database analyze codeql-python-db codeql/python-queries@1.9.0:Security/CWE-089/SqlInjection.ql --format=sarifv2.1.0 --output=python-sql.sarif ``` The expected artifact is a SARIF file with any modeled source-to-SQL paths. Inspect extraction diagnostics first, then the source, sink, and intervening transformations. A finding calls for investigation; absence of a finding does not establish that every request path was modeled. For a confirmed string-built query, use the database API's parameter binding and rerun the same query on a fresh database. Preserve the before/after source, CLI and pack versions, extraction logs, and reports in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). This local result-writing command does not upload SARIF to GitHub. For another language, follow the [language-specific database preparation guide](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/customize-code-scanning/prepare-code-for-analysis), then the [query analysis tutorial](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/customize-code-scanning/analyze-code). Check that language's build, host, and query requirements before reusing a Python procedure. ## Choose the question to investigate Start with the standard security checks. Use custom queries when you need to find variants of a known problem or investigate how data reaches an operation. The [query help](https://codeql.github.com/codeql-query-help/) explains individual checks and their recommendations. ## What to keep in mind Check the support matrix for the language version and framework you use. A successful database creation still needs its diagnostics reviewed for extraction problems. The CLI and the public query libraries have different licensing terms. Check the linked CLI terms before adopting it for a particular repository or service. [Understand static analysis methods](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/#data-flow-and-taint-where-can-an-input-reach) explains what a modeled data-flow path establishes. The system builder currently uses only the Python query above; other catalog languages and query families remain outside its reviewed matching scope. ## Alternatives and complements For Java, [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/) checks compiled class files for bug patterns, while [JBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jbmc/) checks stated properties within configured bounds. Use the [Java workflow guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/) to choose the input and result type that fit your task. - **Summary:** Query a structured model of code to investigate vulnerabilities and trace data flow. - **Use it for:** Use CodeQL to investigate security problems and data flow in a source project, or to write queries for a recurring coding problem. - **What you need:** Create a CodeQL database from source. Some language and extraction modes require a build; others support no-build extraction. documents.title: coverage.py
documents.description: Measure which Python statements and branches a test run executes.
documents.markdown:
# coverage.py

## First try

Use the [coverage fixture](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/#measure-execution-coverage)
to run three small unittest suites against the same Python module. It includes
exact setup and commands, declared source scope, and retained reports.

**Executed with coverage.py 7.10.6 on Windows and Python 3.13.15.** The partial
suite passed its test but left line 9 and the branch from line 3 to line 5
unexecuted. A second suite reached every line and branch without asserting any
return value. The third added assertions. These results separate execution
coverage from the strength of the checks.

## Read the report

`Missing` can name a line or a branch destination such as `3->5`. A function may
have every statement executed while still missing the false path of an `if`.
With branch measurement enabled, the combined percentage includes statements
and branch destinations; read their separate counts as well.

Keep test success, coverage collection, and a configured coverage threshold
separate. A test can pass below the threshold, or fail after executing most of
the source. Confirm that the test process completed and its data was written.
This example measures one process only.

## Use it with other testing methods

[Hypothesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hypothesis/) can generate inputs for properties you define.
Coverage can show which code those tests reached; it does not supply the
properties. [StrykerJS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/strykerjs/) answers a different question for JavaScript:
whether existing tests notice selected changes to the source.

## System builder scope

**Workflow reviewed November 12, 2026.** The builder can suggest one-process
measurement when you have Python source, callable code, and permission to run
the workload. A runnable Python script or module is sufficient; the existing
fixture uses unittest, but coverage.py does not require that runner.

Choose the source directory, branch setting, and existing configuration before
running. The Windows host scope follows the retained fixture; other hosts need
a compatibility check. Subprocess and concurrency collection remain outside
this route. Coverage does not establish that assertions check the behavior.

- **Summary:** Measure which Python statements and branches a test run executes.
- **Use it for:** Find Python code and branch destinations that a selected test run did not execute.
- **What you need:** Provide a working test command, select the source to measure, collect branch data, and retain the data file before generating reports.
- **What you get:** Text, HTML, or JSON reports identify measured statements, missing lines, and missing branches within the configured source scope.
- **Checks and limits:** Executing code does not establish that tests check its result. Process scope, exclusions, and incomplete runs affect the measurement.
- **Finding scope:** Missing lines and branches identify statements and branch destinations not executed in the selected source. A coverage percentage is not a measure of assertion quality or correctness.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Also known as:** Python coverage, coveragepy
- **Analysis mode:** Dynamic
- **What it examines:** Source code, Callable code
- **Context:** Python test suites, Python programs
- **Techniques:** Execution coverage measurement
- **Finding categories:** Execution coverage gaps
- **Where it runs:** A Python runtime supported by the selected coverage.py release. The first example uses coverage.py 7.10.6 and Python 3.13 on Windows.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Python
- **Language support:** Measures Python execution. Native extensions and external services are not covered by the Python source report.
- **Edition and scope:** coverage.py 7.10.6 with standard-library unittest in one Python process. Subprocess, concurrency, and combined-run collection are outside this first workflow.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free local measurement and reporting; test infrastructure can have separate costs.
- **License category:** Open source
- **License:** Apache-2.0 except where noted otherwise in the project notice

Cost information checked 2026-11-06. Runtimes, hosting, and compute may cost extra. Free trials are not counted as free editions.

## Sources and evidence

- [Selected release and Python requirements](https://pypi.org/project/coverage/7.10.6/)

The 80% gate exited 2 for partial coverage and 0 for reach-only coverage. Subprocess collection and assertion quality were not established by coverage percentages.

# Coverity (commercial)

## When to use it

Evaluate Coverity when you need source analysis across a mixed-language codebase and a managed review process. Establish the actual languages, compiler versions, and defect classes you want to compare before using an overall issue count as a metric.

## Worked example: review a C memory defect

**Illustrative evaluation, not run here.** In a small C project, add this function to a file included in its build:

```c
#include <stdlib.h>
void release_twice(void) {
    int *item = malloc(sizeof(*item));
    if (!item) return;
    free(item);
    free(item);
}
```

With an authorized Coverity installation:

1. Configure the C compiler and project using the installed release's instructions.
2. Capture the build and confirm the file was included.
3. Run analysis with the relevant memory checkers enabled.
4. Review any duplicate-release finding and its event path.
5. Remove the second release and compare the results.

This is an evaluation recipe, not a transcript from a licensed run. Commands and server setup depend on the installed product version.

## Commercial versus Scan

[Coverity Scan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/coverity-scan/) has separate eligibility, listed languages, and submission limits. Use that entry when filtering for a free option.

A clean commercial scan still needs evidence that the intended code and configuration were analyzed. For C/C++ verification claims, also compare [Polyspace Code Prover](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/polyspace-code-prover/) and [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/).

## System builder scope

also differ in which files they collect. Source and rebuild access alone do
not establish a supported capture configuration. The broad product language

## What the free option includes

Scan provides a hosted workflow for approved open-source projects. Account and project registration are part of setup. Its local capture tool prepares analysis input; this does not grant an unrestricted license for scanning any private project.

# CPAchecker

## Where it fits

CPAchecker provides another configurable verification workflow beside [CBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cbmc/) and [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/).

## Define the question

documents.title: Cppcheck (Open Source)
documents.description: Find undefined behavior, memory errors, and other defects in C and C++ source code.
documents.markdown:
# Cppcheck (Open Source)

## What it does

Cppcheck examines C/C++ code for defects such as null pointer use, out-of-bounds access, uninitialized variables, and invalid memory management. Its flow-sensitive analysis tracks information about values through code. A finding can identify a correctness problem with security consequences; it does not necessarily establish an exploitable vulnerability.

## Inputs and workflow

You can analyze files directly or import a project configuration, including a compilation database. Build information helps supply the right includes and definitions. Library configuration files describe behavior that the analyzer cannot infer from a declaration alone.

The command-line tool fits local checks and continuous integration. The graphical interface provides another way to configure analysis and browse diagnostics. Findings identify the check and source location; the manual documents text and XML reporting.

## When it is useful

Consider it for native or embedded C/C++ projects, including code with platform-specific definitions. It can complement [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/) because the tools use different analyses and checks.

## Coverage limits

- A different platform or set of preprocessor definitions can expose different code paths. Record which configuration was checked.
- The analyzer deliberately makes tradeoffs that can miss defects. An empty report is not a proof of correctness.
- Open-source MISRA support is partial. Premium offers additional standards coverage and compliance reporting; a tool report alone does not establish product compliance.

## A useful first evaluation

Follow the official manual to import a representative build configuration. Review configuration diagnostics before judging defect findings, then examine a small set of results with the check descriptions. Keep the analyzer version, enabled checks, exclusions, and library configuration with the report.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used Cppcheck for its C and C++ implementations. The reported counts describe those projects and study configurations; they are not validated accuracy measurements or a comparison of Open Source and Premium.

See [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for how to compare scope and useful findings before combining reports.

- **Summary:** Find undefined behavior, memory errors, and other defects in C and C++ source code.
- **Use it for:** Find undefined behavior, memory errors, and other defects in C and C++ source code.
- **What you need:** Source can be checked directly; a compilation database or project import improves build context. Supply includes, macros, target platform, and library models.
- **Checks and limits:** Selected defect checks and partial open-source coding-standard checks. Premium coverage is not inherited by these tags.
- **Finding scope:** Selected defect checks and partial open-source coding-standard checks. Premium coverage is not inherited by these tags.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Source code
- **Context:** Source code
- **Techniques:** Bug finding, Data flow analysis
- **Finding categories:** Memory safety, Logic errors, Coding-standard violations
- **Where it runs:** Windows, Linux, macOS, and other buildable hosts; package availability varies.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** C, C++
- **Language support:** C and C++ source analysis. Configure the target platform, preprocessor definitions, and library models for the build you actually ship.
- **Edition and scope:** Open-source Cppcheck 2.22 and its manual; Premium is compared separately below.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** The open-source analyzer is free, including for commercial code analysis. Cppcheck Premium is a separate paid offering with additional analysis and reporting; its features are not included in this entry's filter tags.
- **License category:** Open source

documents.title: CVE Binary Tool (cve-bin-tool)
documents.description: Identify software components in binaries or dependency inventories and match them to known vulnerabilities.
documents.markdown:
# CVE Binary Tool (cve-bin-tool)

## What it does

CVE Binary Tool first identifies components and versions, or reads an inventory you provide. It then compares that inventory with vulnerability data to report known issues. It can also generate a software bill of materials (SBOM), which lists detected components.

This is software composition analysis (SCA). It belongs in this wiki's static section because it inspects artifacts without exercising the target application. It does not discover a new buffer overflow by reasoning about instructions as [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/) can attempt to do.

## Inputs and ecosystem coverage

| Input                           | Examples                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Binaries and extracted packages | Signatures identify supported components, such as OpenSSL or libpng.                                                                                   |
| Dependency metadata             | Java archives or Maven metadata; JavaScript lockfiles; Python requirements and package metadata; Rust, Ruby, Go, and other documented ecosystem files. |
| Existing inventories            | Component/version lists and supported SPDX, CycloneDX, or SWID SBOMs.                                                                                  |

The language tags are a selected parser inventory. Check the manual for exact filenames, formats, and version-resolution behavior. Recognizing an archive format does not imply recognizing every component inside it.

## Reading the results

Reports associate identified components with advisories and severity information. They support human-readable and structured formats, while triage data and Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) records can preserve reviewed decisions.

A version match is a reason to investigate. It does not demonstrate that the vulnerable functionality is reachable in your application. Component misidentification, backported fixes, missing metadata, and incomplete or stale advisory data can affect results. No findings can also mean a component was not recognized.

## A useful first evaluation

Choose a package with an independently known component inventory, update the vulnerability data, and compare the detected names and versions with that inventory. Review applicability before deciding which findings require an upgrade or mitigation.

For offline operation, prepare the database first and record its age. The manual's offline option prevents live updates; it cannot supply vulnerability records that were never downloaded.

## Related research

**Discussed in a proposed approach:** The [EV charging paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/Sheppard_CSR_2025.pdf) identifies CVE Binary Tool for compiled-code analysis in its ongoing quality-modeling work. The paper is not an accuracy evaluation of component detection or advisory matching.

[Software quality models](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/software-quality/) explains the proposed aggregation and why its conclusions depend on the available measurements. A component/advisory match retains its applicability limits when included in a broader assessment.

- **Summary:** Identify software components in binaries or dependency inventories and match them to known vulnerabilities.
- **Use it for:** Identify software components in binaries or dependency inventories and match them to known vulnerabilities.
- **What you need:** No target rebuild or test harness. Provide binary/package artifacts, manifests, or an SBOM, plus a prepared vulnerability database.
- **Checks and limits:** Matches recognized component identities and versions to advisory data. It does not establish vulnerable-code reachability or discover new code defects.
- **Finding scope:** Matches recognized component identities and versions to advisory data. It does not establish vulnerable-code reachability or discover new code defects.

## Compatibility and scope

- **Analysis mode:** Static
- **What it examines:** Binaries, Dependency metadata
- **Context:** Native binaries, Software packages, Dependency manifests, SBOMs
- **Techniques:** Software composition analysis, Known vulnerability detection
- **Finding categories:** Known vulnerable dependencies
- **Where it runs:** Documented Linux and Windows workflows with Python and format-specific extraction utilities.
- **Languages / ecosystem:** Language independent, Dart, Go, Java, JavaScript, Perl, PHP, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, Swift
- **Language support:** Language tags identify supported dependency ecosystems and metadata parsers, not analysis of application source logic. Binary component detection is language independent and limited to recognizable components.
- **Edition and scope:** CVE Binary Tool repository and user manual; component detection and vulnerability matching, not source-code SAST or exploit testing.

## Cost and editions

- **Cost:** Free
- **Cost conditions:** Free local scanner. Vulnerability data access, extraction dependencies, and any hosted CI service have separate requirements; no paid scanner edition is required for the documented workflow.
- **License category:** Open source
- **License:** GPL-3.0

Cost information checked 2026-09-22. Runtimes, hosting, and compute may cost extra. Free trials are not counted as free editions.
